utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, counsel. If I may take a moment to announce appearances. There are some faces I believe you've not seen before in the courtroom. Start to my immediate right with our new case manager with Sebastian van Hooydonk, who has taken over from Ms. McCreath. Mr. David Re. Mr. Philip Weiner. Ms. Prashanthi Mahindaratne. And Mr. William Fenrick, Senior Legal Advisor to the Prosecution. Thank you very much. And Susan Somers for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We might intrude at that moment to record our condolences to Mr. Weiner on the death of his father -- mother, I beg your pardon. And on a more cheery note, a congratulations to Mr. Petrovic on the birth of his first daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This trial, which has lasted from the middle days of December, broken by the Christmas holidays and picked up in January until very recently, has been a trial that has perhaps been a first in this Tribunal, in that it appears that it is the one case that has a focal point on destruction to cultural property. It is, however, not solely about cultural property. It is about the losses to civilians and civil objects in the course of armed conflict occasioned by the very overt failures of command that were characterised in the second operational group, along with the callous disregard of the troops, officers and soldiers alike, in the 2nd Operational Group of the JNA toward the venerated principle of distinction. The circumstances which provide the background arise out of move by the Republic of Croatia toward independence from the SFRY, the federal army having undertaken actions on the territory of the Republic of Croatia in October of 1991. The focal time for this indictment, of course, is the 6th of December, 1991. In discussing or putting on before the Tribunal, which looks at cases of the most serious violation of international humanitarian law, the importance of the shelling of Dubrovnik on the 6th of December, 1991, was characterised by Prosecution witness Johannes Fietlaars, who said that: "It's not only that within UNESCO the status of Dubrovnik has particularly been pointed out as a city of major importance of human cultural heritage, but also that has played such a central role in European history for almost a thousand years should not be touched like that and should not be destroyed." It goes without saying that the civilian inhabitants of the Old Town of Dubrovnik equally share the protections of international humanitarian law, which were deprived them by the acts and omissions of the accused, Pavle Strugar, commander of the 2nd Operational Group. The root causes, as I have mentioned a few moments ago, are to be found in the failure, the consistent failure of command by the accused as the commander of the 2nd Operational Group and the callous disregard of his subordinates, despite lip service to the contrary for observation -- observance of the principle of distinction. A pertinent part of that principle I will simply take a moment to spell out. "In order to ensure respect for and protection of the civilian population and civilian objects, the parties to the conflict shall at all times distinguish between the civilian population and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives, and accordingly, shall only direct their operations only against military objectives." That did not happen on the 6th of December. The accused was aware on the 6th of December that it had not happened on several occasions before, with the resultant damage to the protected Old Town of Dubrovnik. The accused knew that on 6th December that the command climate which he himself had established -- as does every commander -- the command climate of the 2nd Operational Group was characterised by tolerance of breaches of discipline and criminal activity by his subordinates. About command climate it is said that: "In setting his command climate, the commander reflects the way he is, the way he acts, what he says, what his views are, how he executes command, how he deals with problems." General Andrew Pringle made that clear to this Chamber. The Prosecution has shown beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused on 6th of December knew that he failed in his command of control by leaving in place heavy weaponry which was not justified by military necessity in the hands of his subordinates, who he knew has abused these weapons and engaged in criminal conduct in the recent past. In the totality of the circumstances, he knew to a virtual certainty that under the same circumstances it would be the same result. He failed as a competent and diligent commander; he simply was not one. The Prosecution submits that there was more than just a substantial likelihood that the Old Town would fall victim during the course of any combat on the heights above Dubrovnik with the area around the Old Town. It is -- it was a virtual certainty under the circumstances that had been presented in evidence to this Trial Chamber. There has been a recurring theme of the command of the 2nd Operational Group did not know what was happening, was not aware of such very basic world news such as the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik in November, or the shelling of the Old Town in October. The Prosecution submits that this is an absurd position. This Court has heard evidence and has seen evidence through expert reports that the entire military doctrine for the JNA was based on the commanding officer being informed as much as possible about the overall position. The commanding officer cannot make the excuse that he was not well enough informed regarding a certain event or condition which occurred in a unit under his command. He is himself responsible for the level of information, for making a report to his superior in a timely fashion. Again, on the 6th of December, given the failures of which the accused was aware on the 6th, to have dealt with prior serious violations of international humanitarian law toward the civilian occupants and the civilian objectives in the Old Town -- and by that I mean the rich cultural heritage, its monuments, its ramparts, all that is contained within its legal description -- When, for whatever reason, a conflict broke out on the 6th, the accused new with virtual certainty that it was going to be the same result for the Old Town. He knew it and he did nothing. He did nothing. Another recurring theme which you will hear of throughout today, which you have heard of throughout the past months, is that it was all the responsibility of former co-accused and Prosecution witness of Admiral Miodrag Jokic, the commander of the subordinate unto to the 2 OG, the commander of the 9th GPS. Now, it's clear that the Chamber has had close to a dozen days to hear Admiral Jokic on the witness stand. Admiral Jokic has entered his plea of guilty, has accepted his responsibility and has never at any time in front of this Chamber walked away from that responsibility. He was sentenced before he took the stand and told the Chamber what happened. Who would know better than Admiral Jokic, with no motive to tell anything but the truth? He is a man of almost the same years of the accused and a man who has had to deal with his past. Most importantly, he has accepted his responsibility, has never shown disrespect toward the accused but had indicated he is culpable as well. The responsibility that the accused tries to send back to the Admiral is a continued failure of command, acceptance, responsibility, and indicates that the easy route is to exploit the actions of Admiral Jokic in owning up to his individual criminal responsibility for which he is being punished. The Chamber has heard evidence that the failure by the accused to deal with that with which he was charged as commander of the 2nd Operational Group with respect to undertaking offensives -- excuse me, with respect to his subordinates undertaking further offenses, this failure emboldened his subordinates, both officers and soldiers, to continue to disregard the protected status of the Old Town of Dubrovnik, to disregard orders that appear in this trial to have been nothing more than lip service orders, straw orders, culminating in the absolute disaster of the 6th of December. Now, it is not a numbers game in terms of how many persons were injured or killed or how many structures of great importance to world history were damaged. It is not a numbers game. It is a very serious exercise in observance of a principle of law that could range from a person to a building to thousands of persons to thousands of structures. It is not numbers that should be the focus whatsoever. It is the point of the law was. Indeed, the problems that had existed in this particular operational group were described by the Admiral, by Admiral Jokic, as obvious to any commander, obvious to any command. They were equally obvious to and had to be dealt with by the accused but were not. A recurring theme has been: We had too many problems in the 2nd Operational Group to deal with all the discipline, with all the matters that command responsibility entails. There has been an attempt to mask this as lack of effective control. That is a myth; it is a fallacy. The accused at all times and particularly on the 6th of December had effective control over his subordinate units. The fact that he failed to exercise his ability to command in a proper manner is not tantamount to lack of effective control. It is bad command and nothing more. And that bad command was contagious and seeped all the way down to, as was referred to by General Zorc, the last soldier. Failure to enforce orders, which has been adverted to by not just the experts by Admiral Jokic as well, has very serious consequences on command. In particular, General Zorc indicated: "If orders are given, disobeyed, and nothing is done about it, the real effect of that is that it will begin to create a view at the grassroots level that some orders seem to matter and others don't. And these orders that are flagrantly transgressed and nobody does anything about must therefore be acceptable. It is the green light." "In cases when officers under their command are not experienced enough, or if there are reserve units insufficiently educated in the task, commanding officers tend to become personally involved in controlling and helping those officers under their command," said General Zorc. The accused did not do that. Did not do that. Had an absolute duty to do so, given the nature of his forces, his subordinate forces. Did not do that. And the, result absolutely foreseeably, was the 6th of December, which he knew would result because of October and November incidents. About the concept of command climate. "From the moment a commander walks into his office on the first appointment, he is beginning to set that climate," says General Pringle, "and it reflects the way he is, who he acts, what his view are, how he executes command, how he deals with problems. All that goes to create a climate. What he does when something goes right. What he does when something goes wrong. What action he takes. Does he take a blind eye to certain events or is he a rigorous disciplinarian? All of that encapsulates what is called command climate. We ask the Chamber in its deliberations to review the record and see how absolutely inadequate the command climate that was set on the 2nd Operational Group commander, the accused Pavle Strugar was, and what the consequences of that climate on the 6th of December, which he knew was a continuation of a climate he put into existence, were. This Chamber has heard sufficient evidence that the JNA of the day was an army characterised as a centralised system of command. Orders driven as opposed to strictly initiative-driven armed force. It is, therefore, inconceivable that the things that occurred at lower level emanated strictly from lower level. And in the course of deliberations, we call the Chamber's attention to holding fast to that principle. Discipline was pointed out early on and throughout the case to be a problem, not just with the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade which is the focal battalion for the events of the 6th of December, but throughout the 2OG. Irrespective of the style of command, whether it be orders driven or initiative driven, the higher commander -- but particularly in an orders driven army -- must consider the limitations of the subordinates by thinking "two up, two down"; has to know that the tasks that are being allocated are within the capabilities and the resources of his units; a level of discipline must be a concern of the higher commander in order to enable the absolutely essential smooth functioning of the system of command and control without which there would be anarchy. There would be chaos and anarchy within the units. If a commanding officer fails to take measures against the violation of a disciplinary rules or other orders, this usually creates a favourable climate for such violations to occur. That is exactly what happened on the 6th of December. In such cases, others within the military structure begin practising violence and committing criminal acts, not only against the enemy army, but also against civilians and property protected by international law. I would refer the Chamber to General Zorc's report which is P204 and his testimony at 6485. "Every commanding officer must take responsibility in difficult situations such as the ones which allegedly prevailed in the 2nd Operational Group for the actions of units under his control, which means that he the command must be interested in the actions of the officers and the units under his control, evaluate them, intervene or take personal responsibility for them." This again has been emphatically driven home by General Zorc. As earlier stated, "the commander is responsibility for all those under his command down to the last soldier." The accused, Pavle Strugar, as the highest ranking commanding officer and overall commander of the 2nd Operational Group had a duty to prevent harm to the civilians and the civilian places and items of cultural heritage in the Old Town of Dubrovnik and to punish those of his subordinates who committed acts harming same. He did not carry out his command responsibility. You will hear summation concerning the ordering aspects of the case, the evidence concerning ordering, the aiding and abetting, command responsibility; and the Prosecution submits that the totality of circumstances must at all times be looked to, that this is a dynamic force that is occurring in the 2nd Operational Group and there must be -- that look backward to the extent that it impacts on the mens rea on the 6th of December. The Prosecution draws the Chamber's attention to the fact that despite assurances to very high level representatives of the international community, no disciplinary measures were taken against those perpetrators of the crimes against the civilians and the civilian objects in the Old Town on the 6th of December. Among those who had an absolute affirmative obligation to take those was the accused, Pavle Strugar. The Prosecution will also discuss in the course of its closing submissions Admiral Jokic's acts, Admiral Jokic generally as a witness during the course of this trial, that his acts around the 6th of December and on the 6th of December. And we'll draw the Chamber's attention to why Admiral Jokic's evidence should be accepted, that he put forth his view of what happened on the 6th of December and why it happened. The Chamber should be mindful of the very late shift in theory, or shall we say strategy, by the Defence after the close of the Prosecution case to shift all responsibility to the Admiral. I'm sure the Chamber will take a very careful look at the credibility issues which will be addressed during the course of the submissions, credibility issues of the Defence witnesses. The Chamber will also, I'm confident, bear in mind the strategic political concerns that dominated on the 6th of December, that this was to be the set of comprehensive negotiations advanced at a very high level both in Belgrade and in Zagreb and in the international community and this is the atmosphere in which the command of the 2nd Operational Group and the commander of the 2nd Operational Group had to conduct himself and carry out his mission. I would like to take one moment before I turn the second part over to my colleague to just address a brief moment of appreciation and that would be to all those who have assisted in the presentation, assisted the Prosecution and Chamber in the presentation of this case. That includes the OTP staff in investigations, the leadership research team, the military analysis team, the mapping and visual section for the superb maps that we have been able to provide the Chamber to assist it. The UN security in helping us with our site visit in the Republic of Croatia was outstanding. The representatives of the government of Croatia also assisted. And of course we have the sine qua non, the CLSS interpreting staff, the CVU interpreting staff, as well as the DVU colleagues. And our audiovisual. I would now ask my colleague Mr. Re to proceed on his particular points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My part of the submissions today concern what is commonly called in this Tribunal the crime base. That is, I'm going to talk about what happened in the Old Town on the 6th of December, 1991; that is, what happened from the point of view of those people who were unfortunate enough to be in the Old Town on the 6th of December, 1991, during the sustained JNA shelling. My learned colleague Mr. Weiner will then address you about the military aspects, what actually happened between the two sides in the heights overlooking Dubrovnik, that is in Djakovica, Srdj and the competing versions. We're starting with damage to property and lives first, and then moving to an analysis of how it happened. As Your Honours are very, very much aware, the Old Town of Dubrovnik was entered on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1979. If I could just show -- remind Your Honours, Your Honours probably need no reminding having visited Dubrovnik on a site visit of the Old Town. And we're showing on the screen P17 which is an overhead photograph which displays the Old Town of Dubrovnik. Is it broadcasting, could I ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that is of course the view that Your Honours would have seen in your site visit from the heights above Dubrovnik at Djakovica. Of course this is magnified because Djakovica is some 2 kilometres or so from the Old Town. But looking at that, that is why it is rightly describe as the pearl of the -- or the jewel of the Adriatic. That is a picture of the Old Town as it stands. Now, on the 6th of December, 1991, the residents of the Old Town were awakened at about between 5.30 and 6.00 a.m. in the morning -- Your Honours, just excuse me for one moment. What I will be doing is showing -- demonstrating with several clips from the video exhibits as I go. And my case manager will show them at the right moment. Now, the evidence is that the shelling was first noticed by the residents of the Old Town at a very early moment. People were woken up, firstly by the sound of shelling coming from outside the Old Town. Mr. Weiner will address this in greater detail about the attack or the battle between the Croatian and JNA forces on the out -- on Srdj and -- between Srdj and Djakovica. But the important thing for this is the Old Town, as a UNESCO protected site and of course a civilian object in its entirety, the residents of it were rudely awoken by shells firstly falling outside the Old Town and then inside the outside. Mr. Grbic, for example, described looking out his window and seeing shells falling near Srdj. At 7.00 he described a shell hitting the festival palace which is one of the more significant buildings in the Old Town. Now, if I could remind Your Honours of a clip from P66, which is the compilation from the Croatian television documentary. If Your Honours watch the clip you can see firstly the shelling towards Srdj and then later on the shelling within the Old Town. You can see smoke. You can see roof damage. You can see explosions. The explosion of 31.28 was towards the west of the Old Town. We'll stop there. At 31.34 you can see the view near the Ploce Gate as Your Honours would have seen in your site inspection. The view we're now showing is later, burning boats, again coming from the shelling at a later time, say 9.39. In the overall picture at 31.34 you can now see shows smoke arising from several different places in the Old Town, St. Ivan's fortress. What we're now showing at the end is smoke and shelling outside the Old Town. Now, that's the place in its context of how the residents were awakened on the 6th of December, 1991. Now, why was Dubrovnik on the world heritage list? When it was put on the list in 1979, the Yugoslavian authorities described it quite rightly, as Your Honours would have seen, as: "An urbanistic and architectural gem." World heritage is of course heritage that belongs to the entire world, not just to Croatia. And I want to show Your Honours the extract from the UNESCO report, which is exhibit P63/6 at page 9. It is the introduction to the report that UNESCO -- one of the UNESCO reports after they inspected the damage on the 6th. If I just briefly read to highlight the importance of Dubrovnik in world heritage terms. The first sentence: "Dubrovnik Old Town has primarily been portrayed as an urbanistic and architectural gem," and so on. "This description is undeniably accurate. "And yet Dubrovnik Old Town is so much more than that. Its cultural heritage encompasses archives which Ferdinand Braudel considered the most important source of Mediterranean history. Intact monastic libraries, and a Ragusan school of painting too little known outside specialist circles." And this, this next sentence, is one of the tragedies of what happened on the 6th of December. "However, the observers discovered another form of heritage, a 'movable' form of heritage, which could not claim to be included in any list but which also forms part of the cultural heritage. And they also discovered an intangible heritage of cultural identity, which was paradoxically pointed up by war. The next extract which shows the criteria for nomination is 63/8, the first page. And that is -- if the first paragraph could just be highlighted and broadcast. The criteria for nomination is for the protection of those cultural and natural properties deemed to be of outstanding universal value. It is not intended to provide for the protection of all properties of great interest, importance, or value, but only a select list of the most outstanding of these from an international viewpoint. And on the issue of movable heritage, again, a quote from the UNESCO report, page 63/6 at page 14. That should be 3.1.1. That is something that's often overlooked in what happened in Dubrovnik. It wasn't just the buildings or the people, it was the damage to what is called the movable heritage. UNESCO said: "The wealth of this World Heritage Property is not limited to its immovable heritage but also includes the town archives dating back to 1278." That's 720 years. "The works of art by the Ragusan schools, the monastic libraries, the Franciscan one contained 20,000 books. Then the next paragraph: "There is also a wealth of heritage in private hands which attests the persistence of a collective memories of families, a wealth consisting of furniture, libraries, pictures, maps, scale models of boats and instruments, all of which the observers discovered when visiting houses to survey the damage caused by the various fragments." Now, this was graphically brought home to the Trial Chamber in evidence by Mr. Grbic and Mrs. Ogresta, both of whom lost their houses, Mrs. Ogresta rightly described as a palace in the Dubrovnik style. Mr. Grbic lost his entire collection of artwork, books, and antiquities collected over many, many years. She lost everything in a building of international significance. The shelling continued, as Your Honours have heard, for a large period of the day. One can only imagine the terror that the inhabitants of Dubrovnik must have felt, not knowing whether they were going to live or die, with the sounds of explosions outside, the sounds of shattering glass, roof breaking, detonations, and Mrs. Ogresta graphically described, the smell, the smoke. Witness A also described the smell of the detonations outside and the constant nature of it. And to add to that, the impersonal nature of it. People cowering in their homes and the shelters, wondering: Why are we being attacked? Why are we being shelled? We are a peaceful community of citizens living in a supposedly protected cultural site, yet we are being shelled. Our houses are being destroyed. Our churches are being hit. Our places of religion are being damaged. Our monuments are being hit. There was no doubt that the Old Town -- there was no doubt from the JNA side or the Yugoslavian authorities side, there was not a shadow of doubt that it was entitled to the strongest protections under international humanitarian law and under the 1950 Hague Convention. Your Honours heard evidence from an UNESCO observer there, Dr. Colin Kaiser of his placing emblems, UNESCO-related emblems, and flags around significant buildings and monuments in the Old Town. To demonstrate, to show, and this is in a video taken -- taken when? Excuse me for one moment. This is taken in the -- shown in Exhibit P145, which is the video of the video. The Croatians videoing the JNA on the 8th of December. I'm just going to show you the very beginning of that video to remind the Trial Chamber that these emblems were, in fact, quite evident from outside of the Old Town. Your Honours can see in the first clip there is an emblem on the Sponza Palace. Your Honours can also see the roof damage to the Sponza Palace, demonstrated by the blue tarpaulin covering it. Your Honours can also see on the clip we were just showing is there -- we are just stopping here another indication of a cultural property or cultural emblem on St. Blaise Church, or St. Vlaho's Church, which was directly opposite the Sponza Palace. Now, of course Your Honours have seen in the videos the UN flag or UNESCO flag flying over Minceta. It was quite apparent to all in the surrounding area, and especially those on the heights overlooking as witness B told the Trial Chamber, it was particularly evident that the signs of protection were flying and especially in the wind it was even more evident, the blue and white flag was even more evident. If I could just perhaps put a page on the ELMO. It's Article 9, 10, and 11 of The Hague Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in the event of armed conflict. And if I could also put the other page which is Article 16. Perhaps if you could put Article 16 first, Mr. Usher. Article 16 refers to the emblem of the convention and the use of the emblem. Your Honours see the description there of the emblem certainly matches what we've just seen in Exhibit P145. That is the distinctive emblem of the convention, a shield, sapphire blue and white. Thank you. If you could now place the next sheet on the ELMO which is Articles 9, 10, and 11. I take Your Honours, in the context of emblems, to Article 9 of the convention which is under chapter 2 under Special Protection, and that sets out the immunity under special protection. And that is "high contracting parties undertake to ensure the immunity of cultural property under special protection by refraining ... from any act of hostility directed against such property except for the cases provided for in paragraph 5 of Article 8, which refers to renunciation of the rights." And of course there is no evidence and it's certainly not the case that there was any renunciation of the rights afforded to the Old Town of the special protection. If you then move to Article 11, withdrawal of immunity. It sets out how an opposing party is released from immunity in the case of a violation. But it says at the last sentence of Article 1 -- sorry 11.1, "nevertheless, whenever possible, the latter party shall first request the cessation of such violation within reasonable time." Now, of course reasonable time is not defined there. And at Article 2, the last sentence: "Whenever circumstances permit, the opposing party shall be notified, a reasonable time in advance, of the decision to withdraw immunity." Now, I raise this because of the Defence submission at paragraph 617 of the Defence submissions on the Article, where the Defence has indicated that somehow the Old Town has been deprived of protection. And they go on to say: "The Defence points to the assertions made in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal in relation to the special status and withdrawal of immunity of cultural property." And then quote the Kordic case. The difficulty with that submission, Your Honours, is that the circumstances have in no way given rise to withdrawal of immunity or notification under Article 11.1 or 11.2. The opposing party, that is the JNA or the Yugoslav forces, considered that this immunity would be withdrawn. It's just not there. And the Prosecution certainly submits that if the Old Town had been used in violation of the protections under the Convention, and it certainly was not, the other side, the JNA, would have been obliged under the convention to notify the Croatian authorities that they considered that the Old Town was being used in violation of the convention and that immunity would be withdrawn or should be revoked. That didn't happen. The next section I wish to deal with are the specific crimes alleged the Prosecution now says are proved beyond a reasonable doubt occurring in the Old Town on the morning or the day of the 6th of December, 1991. The Prosecution has charged the accused with responsibility for the deaths of two young civilian men, Mr. Urban, Mr. Pavo Urban, and Mr. Tonci Stocko. There was not a shred of evidence, and we will address this later, not a shred of evidence that these young men were anything other than civilians, not taking a direct part in hostilities on the morning. The Defence has taken issue with the fact of the death of both. At page 105 at paragraph 504, the Defence submission says: "The Defence challenges the allegation that the persons designated in the indictment have perished in the Old Town at the time, place, and in the manner described in the indictment." The Prosecution submits that the evidence of their deaths in the Old Town of Dubrovnik on the morning of the 6th of December, 1991, is absolutely overwhelming. The Prosecution has produced direct, the most direct evidence possible of the death of Mr. Tonci Stocko and has produced compelling circumstantial evidence of the death of Mr. Pave Urban in the Old Town on that morning. I remind Your Honours of Exhibit P55, which is a paragraph shown to Witness Mato Valjalo. Your Honours can see that Mr. Valjalo who is of course one of the victims of the serious injury, the cruel treatment, has marked on this exhibit with the X in the middle where he was when he was running through the street and the Old Town at about 9.00 or so in the morning when a shell exploded behind injuring him. If Your Honours look at where the photograph is taken, the photograph is taken from right next to the Sponza Palace below the bell tower. Now, the importance is shown in the next exhibit which is the photograph of Mr. Pave Urban's body lying underneath the bell tower. And this was the photograph identified by Witness A who looked out his window to the right. Your Honours would have seen the location from where Witness A saw it, which is probably about 40 to 50 metres from the body, and identifying this body as that of the one that he saw lying under the clock tower on that particular morning. It's also in Exhibit P66 at about time of 32, where the body is shown and there is a car speeding around the corner there. If Your Honours look at the photo there and the post mortem photograph which shows the same -- a person wearing the same clothes. Of course -- before it goes -- it's gone now, you can see the camera lying at Mr. Urban's left shoulder. If you compare the post mortem photograph, you can see a person, Mr. Urban, is wearing the same clothes. And of course you've got Dr. Ciganovic's evidence of the cause of death. So if you put everything together, the circumstantial case, in the Prosecution's submission, is overwhelming. This man was taking photographs in the Old Town. Mr. Mustac saw him walking around at that time with his camera. Witness A saw him dead under the bell tower some hours later. Shells has exploded in the Stradun over that period of time. Your Honours have seen videos of the shell pockmarks throughout the Stradun. And the person on the table in the mortuary and the cause of death are all entirely consistent with the cause of death Prosecution -- with him dying from shell -- dying as a result of shell injuries. Now, the Defence at paragraph 449 took issue with part of Dr. Ciganovic's report. And the Prosecution of course recognises the limitations of a report when someone is doing 19 autopsies in one day in very, very difficult conditions as described by Dr. Ciganovic: No running water, variable electricity and being ordered by the investigating judge to perform external examinations. The Defence at paragraph 499 said "the explosive wounds can only be the mechanism of injuring which had caused death but they cannot be the cause of death itself. The mechanism of death is one thing; the cause of death quite a different one. One cannot give the finding that the cause of death is an explosive wound or injury." What Your Honours of course realise is that completely ignores is the evidence of their own medical expert, Dr. Soc, who came here to criticise severely Dr. Ciganovic's report but without having had the benefit of seeing the transcript of the proceedings or being aware of the entirety of the evidence. And when we put to Dr. Soc in cross-examination the scenario, which is basically unchallenged on the evidence before this Trial Chamber, this is what he said: "A shell exploding 40 to 50 metres away from a person, exploding with fragments flying about, fragments could enter a person and kill them or cause an injury leading to their death." To which he answered: "That's right." The next question was: "You may expect to see an explosive wound from a flying shrapnel. I say may." To which the answer was: "It may be the case, yes." The next question was: "And a shell exploding close to a person could cause blast injuries and kill them instantly, couldn't it?" To which Dr. Soc's candid answer -- which was basically the only one that he, as a medical practitioner experienced in both autopsies and the treatment of war victims, could say -- was: "That may be another circumstance involved. That's beyond doubt. Lives can be lost when a person is hit by shrapnel from as for away as 40 metres from where the person is actually standing." Now, that, Your Honours, is the importance of which Mr. Valjalo marked. Because in combination with what Mr. Mustac says where he saw Mr. Urban, that places Mr. Urban well and truly within range of where shells were exploding in the Stradun. Of course Your Honours are aware of the large shell crater in front of St. Blaise's Church, which is the subject of much cross-examination and examination in chief with Dr. Vilicic. That may well have been the cause of Mr. Urban's death. We will never know. There are certainly shell marks consistent in that area with, as Dr. Soc, concedes, an explosion which could have caused his death. The Prosecution says: The only inference that can be drawn is that Mr. Urban died on that day in that spot as a result of a shell exploding and a shell fired from JNA positions. That's Mr. Urban. Now, the Defence of course will not even concede the fact of death or the manner of death of Mr. Stocko, even though they make the concession in their brief that it was the JNA. They say the 9th VPS and the 3rd of the 472nd Brigade which were firing shells into the Old Town. The evidence of Mr. Stocko's death is basically unchallenged. There was an eyewitness to it. Mr. Jovic who was injured by flying shrapnel was injured himself by a shell that exploded some 40 or so metres away at the best estimate, consistent with Dr. Soc's evidence of what could kill a person and was with Mr. Stocko when he collapsed a minute later, with what Mr. Jovic described when his t-shirt was lifted up as seeing a hole in the man's, in the deceased chest, with blood. I want to show you the autopsy photograph of Mr. -- when it comes on to the screen you will see that the injury which is depicted to the chest of the deceased is not only consistent with what Mr. Jovic said but fits in with all the other evidence of the shelling and the causes of death. While that's coming up on the screen, I'll just point to the extract I read from Dr. Soc's evidence at 7977 and 7978 of the transcript. We seem to be having a technical problem with Sanction. I'll come back to this, if time permits, at a later stage. The next challenge to the Prosecution evidence was in relation to the injuries sustained by Mr. Valjalo and Mr. Vlasica, again civilians going about their business in the Old Town on the morning of the 6th of December, 1991. The technical problems have been overcome and I'll just broadcast for one moment the photograph of Mr. Stocko which is an exhibit at page -- are Your Honours getting a signal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. I gather the technicians are working on the matter at the moment, Mr. Re. Perhaps you would move on to the injuries --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm doing just that. I won't deal with the issue of the medical reports or the differences in the medical reports. Those were, in my submission, well and truly cured in Dr. Soc's evidence and his concessions, and we've covered that in our final trial brief. What I do want to address is what the Defence has said about Mr. Vlasica's credibility. He was a civilian shop keeper who was standing in the doorway of his shop in Od Puca when a shell exploded nearby just as with Mr. Stocko, and he was injured by shrapnel on the morning. The Defence attacks his credibility at page 497 -- sorry, paragraph 498 by saying that: "Although allegedly seriously wounded, when he was transferred to the hospital, while lying down in his vehicle which was transporting him, he registered down to every detail all the damages that were present in the Old Town." The Defence upholds that it is difficult to believe that anyone to seriously wounded to have listed all the serious damages. In the Prosecution's submission, that is a serious misrepresentation of the evidence and Mr. Vlasica's credibility cannot be attacked on that basis. At page 3325 he simply said: "As we were going through Od Puca street, I noticed a fire ablaze to my left," meaning I saw houses burning, houses opposite the orthodox church. "There was an incredible amount of material on the streets so that the driver had to dodge the rubble, the bricks, the debris on the floor -- pavement rather. I know he arrived at the Pile gate. That's all I remember. I don't recall anything else because at that moment I faded and only came to at the hospital." The Defence also submitted that the -- as a most curious submission by attempting to import, one would think, the concept of volenti non fit injuria, or voluntary assumption of risk into international humanitarian law. That's at paragraph 505, where the Defence submits that because the general alarm had sounded every citizen had an obligation "in accordance with the possibilities," whatever that means, to comply and take protective cover. It was basically a way -- and then they moved on to say that Mr. Urban and Mr. -- or the persons outside who perished were not respecting the general alarm, that's at 508, they were moving outside the protective shelters, constantly placing themselves and their health at risk, having thus contributed to the serious consequences that ensued. "Then there's a particularly callous submission, in the Prosecution's submission. They then go on at 509 to say: "If these men had perished -- if they had really perished on the 6th of December in the Old Town, then they to an enormous degree have contributed to the occurrence of serious consequences." This of course isn't a negligence case, it's a case of serious violations, the most serious violations of international humanitarian law. The Prosecution submits that these fanciful submissions should be disregarded in their entirety. The Prosecution says they should never have been made. They don't form part of the law. There is no Defence based on voluntary assumption of risk. In relation to the submission at 507, that "not a single person in the Old Town had perished in the shelter, also not a single person that was located in any housing building in the Old Town, regardless of its construction characteristics, was either wounded or killed. The Prosecution's response to that, well that is just only a matter of luck. The clear evidence is that the shelter, the Simoni school was actually hit on the day. The school is on the corner only 40 metres from where Tonci Stocko and Mr. Jovic were hit by flying shrapnel. It was only a matter of luck, in the Prosecution's submission, because of the solid nature of the building. The people were just lucky the walls were made of stone and not wood. Had the Old Town been of wooden construction, the damage to life and property would have been far, far, far greater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient point, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It would be, Your Honour, we might be able to fix the technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. What we will do then is resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Technical difficulties resolved, I move to the issue of what I can call the property damage, which is the subject of counts 4, 5, and 6 of the third amended indictment. Mr. Fenrick will address in greater detail on the law which we have covered in detail on attacks on civilian objects and devastation by military necessity and damage to cultural property. The Prosecution's submission is: When you look at the evidence in its entirety of the damage to the Old Town, the property damage to the Old Town, on the day the only -- the overwhelming evidence -- the overwhelming inference, everything points to one thing: That it was damaged and it was damaged due to JNA or 2nd Operational Group shelling on that day. The evidence before the Trial Chamber of damage before that day was of minor damage in October and November, again from 2OG shelling. But damage which was easily distinguished, and the witnesses said this, from what occurred on the 6th of December throughout the day. The damage could not have been caused by anything else. The shelling is the only thing that could have caused it. The video evidence, the eyewitness evidence only points to one thing. The evidence of building rubble strewn throughout the streets. The buildings with holes in their roofs. Large holes caused by shells. The shrapnel damage could only have been caused by one thing, and that is shelling. It's also the location of damage throughout the Old Town. The extent of the damage and the type of the damage. When you put it all together, the only conclusion is that it was the 2nd Operational Group's shelling which caused it. The Prosecution's submission is that we have established beyond a reasonable doubt what is really only a representative sample of the damage that occurred in the Old Town on that day, but for the purposes of this Prosecution it suffices. The Prosecution respectfully and happily adopts Your Honours -- the Trial Chamber's annex to its Rule 98 bis decision. And in annex 4 to our final trial brief, as Your Honours have seen, we have marked all the buildings on that which Your Honours have found at 98 bis level. There was sufficient evidence at 98 bis level. The Prosecution says that in the absence of any evidence contradicting that of the extent, type location of property damage in relation to all the buildings in the annex of the 98 bis decision, the Prosecution has established beyond a reasonable doubt that the damage caused to each of those buildings on the 6th of December was caused by JNA shelling. There's one brief addition to that which I note in oral submissions, and that is we have placed a C1 on the institute building, which is the building opposite the Dominican monastery, where the evidence which was found in Dr. Kaiser's evidence, of his being there on the day when it was shelled and damaged. That's the only additional building we take Your Honours to. What I want to look at is the pattern of damage and I turn to religious damage as just one category of damage to buildings throughout the Old Town. I'm showing you an extract from the UNESCO report, 63/9, and it's a map showing the damage to religious structures throughout the Old Town. With the exception of the one which is marked number 7, which is the bottom left-hand corner, which isn't in the indictment, it shows a pattern of destruction to the other 12 religious buildings ranging from 10 Catholic institutions there to the Orthodox church and of course the synagogue. All of those buildings are marked on annex 4. All of them are included in the annex to the Rule 98 bis decision. But this shows the distribution of damage just to religious buildings throughout the Old Town on the 6th of December, 1991. Just taking you briefly to several specific sites, if I could just take Your Honours to the Franciscan monastery. I'm going to show you a 10-second clip from P145. Now, this building is of course a very large building, and according to the UNESCO report was built in -- the building was started in 1317 and its most beautiful cloisters were built around 1348. The UNESCO report -- that's P63/9 at page 36 -- refers to it being hit by 37 shells. There's no reason to doubt that if one looks at the videos showing the damage, the holes in the roofs. The three videos all show hole damage to the roof. But what I want to show you at 8.10 to 8.20 is to remind you of the evidence what caused the damage. And you can see in this clip, you can see damage to the interior of the Franciscan monastery and you can see a person holding a shell, the tail end of -- keep going -- the tail-end of a shell which had come through the roof. There is the video of the JNA representatives filming it the day following -- two days after the bombing or the shelling. You can see people holding shells. And in this, picture at 8.40, tail fins. You can clearly see tail fins from the 37 impacts described in the report. The holes are also demonstrated by the Dominican monastery, which as I showed you on the map before, is at the other end of the Old Town, which is at the Ploce Gate end. One photo most graphically demonstrates that is at P10 which is the colour slides attached to P63/6 and that is photograph P13. Suffice it to say that each of these religious structures was built between the 11th century, in the case of the Sigurata Church, and the mid-19th century in the case of the Orthodox church. I mention in passing the mosque which isn't on that map, the UNESCO map, but it was inspected by Mr. Vukovic. It was also damaged on the day. It was in Miha Pracata. It was A39 on annex 4. It was 25 metres or so from where Mr. Stocko was killed. That brings me to a most curious submission, if I can put it in those terms, in the Defence submission, and that is at paragraph 518. That is -- I suppose one could loosely term it an arson conspiracy theory, in which the Defence submission or final trial brief says: "Out of six buildings that had allegedly burned down, five were owned by persons from Serbia or Montenegro." It then goes on to list the buildings allegedly owned by persons from Serbia or Montenegro. And it concludes with the grandest conspiracy theory suggestion of all: "The Defence finds that this, in fact, more than just a pure coincidence which must be taken into consideration in evaluating the events that are the subject of this deliberation." The difficulty with this submission, apart from the fact that it is purely speculative, is the fact that there is simply no evidence of it. What is the Defence submission suggesting? That there was arson by the Croats? That there was some conspiracy to set fire to property which may have been Serb owned? Well, it's not quite coming to the point. But the fallacy of this, apart from the fact that there is no evidence to the Trial Chamber apart from the ownership of these particular buildings or these particular shops or whatever, is that it ignores the fact that the Serbian Orthodox church directly opposite the buildings that burnt down -- one of them allegedly owned by the Serb but there's no evidence of that -- was hit on the roof by shells. There's a photo at page 52 of Exhibit P63/9 -- that's the UNESCO report -- which shows the Serbian Orthodox church with holes in the roof, which could only have been caused by shelling from the 2nd Operational Group. And if there had been any suggestion that the Croatians had been setting fire to Serb-owned building, why is that not in P61/39, that is the letter or the report made by the JNA two -- several days afterwards? Would that not have been the most marvelous opportunity to demonstrate that the Croatians had done it themselves? Well, if that were true, one would expect it to be there and it's not. It also ignores that we have no idea of what percentage of the many, many other buildings damaged in the Old Town were Serbian, Montenegrin, or otherwise owned. The Prosecution submits the most important thing, the consideration from this particular submission, is the fact that the Defence cannot even concede the fact of destruction even though they could not challenge it in cross-examination of these buildings on that particular day. To demonstrate the spread of buildings, as found in annex 4 -- that the Prosecution says that it can prove that there is direct evidence beyond a reasonable doubt, I take you to annex 4 of the final trial brief. That of course shows buildings throughout the town on both sides. It shows damage to the pavement of the Stradun. It shows damage to the Old Port -- that's at B1 on the right. It shows damage to monuments such as the Onofrije Fountain at A7 to the left. It shows damage to the walls, to the northern walls, to the western walls. It shows damage to 15 religious buildings and it shows damage to many, many houses where people were sheltering on the day. The Prosecution's submission -- and I conclude on this note -- is that the only inference available, and it is overwhelming, is that the Prosecution has proved beyond a reasonable doubt damage to each of those buildings and it was caused by JNA shelling, 2nd Operational Group shelling, and there can be no other cause. And the Prosecution submits that it has proved its case insofar as the death, injuries, cultural property damage, attacks on civilians, and attacks on civilian objects in relation to the crime base. That completes my portion of the submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will address what happened on December 6th. I'll begin by providing an overview of the attack and then very briefly describe the JNA positions. From there, I will discuss the Croatian military positions. We will confront the allegations of Croatian military weapons within the Old Town. We will discuss the positions surrounding the Old Town, and finally, we'll finish with who shelled the Old Town. The plan of attack, according to the evidence, of the Croatian fortress at Mount Srdj was implemented on the 6th of December, 1991. The attack on the fortress came from two directions: From the left or from the west it came from -- at about 5.00, Zoran Lemal led a unit of infantry from the 2nd Operational Group across from Strincjera from Mount Srdj. One hour later, Croatian military positions on Srdj were shelled by 2nd Operational Group guns. At 6.20 Budimir Pesic led another infantry group, from the right this time, or the east, from Basanka to Srdj. As Pesic moved 2 to 400 metres towards Srdj, they came under fire from Croatian mortars. Around 7.00 shells were landing in the Old Town. Around 7.20, three shells had struck the Grbic home and it had started to burn.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry. By 8.00 a.m. Zoran Lemal's unit were 4 to 600 feet from the repeater on Mount Srdj and they had signaled their units to start any firing so it won't hurt their own men. At that time, Pesic radioed to have the mortar fire on his side stopped, meaning the JNA fire on Srdj. From 7.45 to 8.30 in the morning, when 120-millimetre mortars from the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade were shelling various positions in Dubrovnik and the surrounding areas in Lapad and Babin Kuk. At 8.00, Pesic's unit enters the Sdrj area. Between 8.00 and 8.30 one of Lemal's soldiers is killed. Between 8.00 and 8.30 a request is made for 130-millimetre guns from Cilipi to fire. At approximately 8.36 a.m., that request is denied. At 8.30, Budimir Pesic, the leader of the squad that came from Bosanka is injured. At 9.00, there is strong mortar fire on Srdj from the Croatian side. Lemal loses three men. Also around this time Slavoljub Stojanovic arrives and takes command of Pesic's unit. At 9.30 there's another request for 130-millimetre mortars to fire. That request was denied at 9.50. At 11, Lemal is taking more casualties. General Strugar orders the 2nd Operational Groups to cease fire at 11.15. Sometime at either 11.00 or 12.00, Stojanovic withdraws his unit back toward Bosanka. At 11.30, the Croatian mortars at the SDK building are out of ammunition, but their mortars at Babin Kuk continue to fire. At 11.45, the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade stops firing. They do continue firing sometime in the afternoon. In the afternoon, Captain Kovacevic orders Mr. Lemal's unit to withdraw. Stojanovic's unit returns to their base in Bosanka between 1 and 2 p.m. According to Witness B, the firing at Djakovica stopped at 3.00. All shelling ends around 7.15 p.m., according to the ECMM monitors. During that day, the Old Town was struck by 82-millimetre mortar shells. It was struck by 120-millimetre shells, Maljutka missiles and recoilless cannon fire. In the early afternoon, at 12.43 p.m., we see on Exhibit P66 the Old Town of Dubrovnik. You can see the smoke coming out. And that's at 32 minutes, 15 to 19 seconds. Later that afternoon, this so-called jewel of the Adriatic looked like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is at 32 minutes, 23 to 28 seconds. That's what it looked at as the sun was starting to go down. The Old Town was within the firing range of the following 2nd Operational Group units: We know Djakovica, the 120-millimetre battery at Uskoplje, also referred to as Ledenica; the 82-millmetre mortar battery at Strincjera; Admiral Jokic says the 82-millimetre battery at Bosanka; and finally, there's discussion of another battery, an 82-millimetre battery at Racevica. Mr. Vilicic mentions this in his testimony and in his report at pages 5 to 6. Witness B also seems to describe this, because he says that they were firing Maljutkas and recoilless cannons from Zarkovica, but from behind Zarkovica, there were mortars. And if you look at a map, Racevica is behind Zarkovica. Now, where with the Croatian military positions? First, it's our contention that there were no Croatian military positions in the Old Town of Dubrovnik. Three Defence witnesses have testified to observing weapons in the Old Town on the 6th of December. A number of witnesses have denied seeing any weapons or any outgoing fire from the Old Town on December 6th, and those witnesses included local residents; former JNA soldiers; and independent observers such as Pur, Valkov and Colin Kaiser. Further, the Prosecution submits that the Defence testimony on this issue is not credible. Let's consider each of those three witnesses. First we have Mr. Vladimir Pepic. He's the witness who testified that his eye sight was better than that of a zoom lens. With the naked eye standing 50 metres behind the front of Djakovica, from approximately 2300 miles away, he claims that he saw an anti-aircraft gun near the turret towards the front of the entrance and he saw an 82-millimetre mortar between the wall and the water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mean metres rather than miles, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Now, if we look at Exhibit P66 at 1306 seconds we see the recoilless cannon and the camera right above the recoilless cannon. And if you notice at that point you cannot even see boats in the harbour. Now, let's continue to 13 minutes and 15 seconds and stop as they use the zoom lens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Even with the zoom lens it would be difficult to see an object such as a mortar. And you probably couldn't see an anti-aircraft gun. Even the boats look like small squares. His fellow Defence witness, Budimir Pesic, testified that you could not see a mortar from that distance with the naked eye, and that's at 7924. And he said even with binoculars at that distance you could not determine the calibre of the mortar. That's at 7926. In addition to seeing a mortar, Mr. Pepic wants you to believe that they moved into open view in front of the 2nd Operational Groups on Djakovica and then hit another mortar. They rolled it out and then hit it. We suggest this testimony isn't even plausible. Further, neither the mortar nor the anti-aircraft gun are visible in video P66. If we begin at 7.13 a.m. That's 31 minutes and 7 seconds and stop at 31 minutes and 19 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: 31 minutes and 19 seconds. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that's being considered, did you mean Mr. Pesic or Mr. Pepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic. However, Mr. Pesic testified also about what you could see at certain distance, because he was looking at a similar distance from up on Srdj towards Babin Kuk and he said he could not see mortars at 2.000 metres without binoculars. He said at that distance you couldn't see a mortar without binoculars. And even with binoculars, Mr. Pesic said, you could not determine the calibre of the mortar, which is in conflict with Pepic's, Vlado Pepic's testimony, because he says not only could he see with the naked eye, he could see the calibre of the mortar. Now, we're stopped here, sometime after 7.00 at 31 minutes and 19 seconds. There is no anti-aircraft gun visible nor is any mortar visible in front. Now, if we continue to 31 minutes please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Again we see a view from the side, and again, there is no anti-aircraft gun as we look from the side up in the turret or any mortar appears to be moving out front. The witness further claims -- the witness is Vladimir Pepic -- that he saw some flashes two-thirds of the way down the Stradun. On a side street -- and the flashes were coming out of a buildings on a side street. From these flashes he assumes it was a mortar firing. And again he claims he saw this with the naked eye. We're talking over 3.000 metres. As you recall, at those first video pictures we showed just above the recoilless weapon, you couldn't even see the entrance area or the harbour area of the Old Town clearly. And he expects us to be able to see flashes some 5 to 700 metres farther away. Mr. Pepic further states that the flashes were 6 to 7 metres long, and that's at 7559, and they ran from the bottom of the building up to the top. Now, his fellow witnesses disagree with these type of facts. Witness Nesic says that a flame from a mortar is only 1 and a half metres long. That's at 8205. Mr. Drljan says that the flash from a mortar is only 1 metre long and that's at 7113. No one is saying that a flash from a mortar is 6 to 7 metres long and it would radiate from the bottom to the top of a building. The Prosecution submits that there was no mortar seen by Mr. Pepic. There was no great radiation, radiating flash, nor could he have been a mortar or an anti-aircraft gun near the Old Town entrance. His testimony is just not credible. The second witness, Jovan Drljan, also made observations that are not credible. He testified that he saw flashes behind the Orlando column, which he believed to be coming from a mortar. And then halfway down the Stradun he sees a mortar being pulled out to the street; there for one minute, it fires, and it's pulled back. Like Mr. Pepic he also claims to have superhuman eyesight. When he's questioned about these flashes at 7754, he's questioned and answers the following: "And this, in fact, whatever you saw was at a distance of about approximately 3.000 metres from an elevation and behind the pillar?" Answer: "This event took place behind the pillar and you can see the flame clearly. I've been doing that for 17 years. I've sailed for 17 years and my eyesight is very sharp because I trained my eyesight with sailing. When I see something at that sort of distance, I just can't go wrong." Now, he changes his testimony at one point at pages 7731 and 32 and concedes that it might have been shells falling that caused the flashes. 7731 and 32. Further, we've seen that unless there is a dark background, if the area is in shadows or its dark outside, you can't even see the flashes that emanate from a mortar. At P219 there are two photographs which you'll see, which were taken of mortars firing and you can't see the flashes. In our case, where we did show photographs of a flash of the mortars firing, one is against a dark background of trees and the other was in an area that was under the shadow of trees. And also, the photograph was taken close. When you take a photograph close up to the mortar that's firing, you can also see that 1 to 1 and a half metre flash. Here you can see that you don't see how we see the flame, especially in a bright area. Now, the witness testified that he could see that and it was a bright sunny morning. His second statement is also suspect. He claims that they dragged this mortar; within a minute it fired. Even the Defence witnesses have testified that you cannot fire a mortar off of a hard surface unless you put padding, bracing, sandbags. You have to prepare the surface. Now, the witness indicated, as I said, it was fired within one minute after it was placed on the Stradun and he did not see any sort of padding, bracing. Nothing was placed under it. Firing in this situation is not plausible. Further, there is no other witness that corroborates Mr. Drljan's testimony. No one else saw this sudden mortar coming out of some doorway. No one else saw this flashing by the Orlando Hotel. Finally what's interesting is this witness was responsible for placing entries in the war diary. He claims to have made an interesting observation, seeing one and possibly two mortars in the Old Town, but he never places these in the log. We submit he never placed them because they never occurred. We submit that his testimony isn't credible and it should be rejected. Finally, Nikola Jovic claims to have seen three weapons in the Old Town. First he claims to have seen a mortar at the southern-most turret of the Old Town. And he claims that he neutralised it with one cannon recoilless projectile. That's at 8238. The problem is -- I'm sorry. There is a mistake in the transcript, it's my mistake. At 31.1 it says Nikola Jovic. It should be Novica Nesic. 29.1, yes. Mr. Nesic claims that he neutralised that. The problem is Nesic doesn't mention this mortar in his ammunition expenditure report, which is D13. Nor does he mention it in the combat report or in the subsequent report filed, D65. But what is more significant is the method in which he neutralised this weapon. He claims to have used a recoilless cannon. The turret which he claims he hit is far beyond the maximum range of this weapon. Professor Vilicic, who is one of the designers of this particular recoilless weapon explained it has a range of up to 1.000 metres and is intended for targets of 600 metres. He stated a shell from it can travel up to 2.000 metres. But then he added at page 8430 that shells from a recoilless cannon: "could reach, at a stretch, up to a length of 2.000 metres." The turret in question is on the southern-most side about halfway or mid-way through the Old Town. It's approximately 3.000 metres. Nesic's weapon could not reach that. It could barely reach 2.000 metres, let alone another 1.000 metres into the Old Town. That claim cannot be given any merit. Nesic also claims that he had seen an anti-aircraft gun in the window to the right of the harbour entrance. He says he never saw the barrel, he only saw flashes and from the flashes he believes it to be an anti-aircraft gun. Nesic's testimony on this is conflicting. He claims to have seen the gun at around noontime, which is at transcript 8172. But he claims to have neutralised this same weapon in the morning, at 8236. Again, there is no mention of this weapon in his ammunition expenditure report, D113, nor is it mentioned in the combat report or the report filed subsequently thereafter, D65. There is not one witness who corroborates the existence of this weapon. According to the ECMM monitors, there was no outgoing fire from the Old Town on that date, December 6th, nor do the monitors observe any traces from an anti-aircraft gun emanating out of the Old Town. As you recall, they are staying at the Argentina Hotel. They are overlooking -- they are on the water and they are overlooking the Old Town. There is no evidence that they observed any traces. Finally, Nesic wants us to believe that an anti-aircraft gun weighing hundreds of kilograms and having one or two long barrels was moved into a building and fired without anyone other than him seeing this, seeing any of this. The Prosecution submits that common sense tells you that this observation is highly suspect. Nesic finally claims that he saw some men moving from the harbour area into the Old Town and that they were carrying crates, these long crates which he claimed to be familiar with, the types used to carry ammunition. He doesn't say that they were running. He doesn't say that they were rushing. Further, he claims that they're doing this out in the open while the shelling is occurring. No other Defence witness sees this; no other Prosecution witness sees this. No ECMM monitor sees this. If we look at P61 page -- at document 30, when it comes up -- these are the notes of Per Hvalkof, which he wrote, or he drafted, based on the information he receives from the other monitors. They're watching the shelling. They're counting the explosions. They even see their vessel, Argosy in flames out on the water. But there's no record of people with ammunition crates in the area where the shells are landing. There's no record of any group of men walking in and out of the entrance to the Old Town. The witness even notes the absurdity of this situation by describing similar circumstances. He was asked if soldiers would move an anti-aircraft gun in broad daylight and he says -- this is at page 8627: "Not a single soldier in a theater of war would be crazy enough to be doing something in broad daylight when they can be seen by anybody." He wants us top believe that this occurred when no soldier would commit any similar act. That's what Nesic wants you to believe. The Prosecution submits that Nesic's testimony concerning his observations of military activity is not credible, in fact, it's fraudulent and we'll explain why. He came up with phantom targets to cover his actions. This is obvious when reviewing the ammunition expenditure report which is D113. That's corroborated by both Pepic and Nesic. Witness B tells us that Kovacevic used the phone on Djakovica. He saw him do it a couple of item times, use that hand-held phone. That's corroborated by Pepic. Witness B tells us there were flags flying over the Old Town. He didn't understand what the flags were. He asked some of the others and they said: Those are protected buildings. That's corroborated by the videos and Colin Kaiser. Witness B tells us to shelling began on Srdj and shifted to the Old Town. That's corroborated by Negodic and it's also corroborated by the video, Exhibit P66. Witness B tells us that infantry moved towards Srdj. What do we know about it from witness Pesic? We know that's true. We know that he went from Bosanka towards Srdj. Witness B tells us that the troops of the 2nd Operational Group -- or he says the JNA troops in Zarkovica -- fired at windows, vessels, walls. That's also corroborated by the video. Very important piece of testimony. Remember him mentioning that while he was on Djakovica, three Croatian shells landed in the area around Djakovica but didn't fall on the area of the JNA troops. In fact, he was 19 years old at the time and he admitted, what did he do? He ran in one of the buildings for shelter and he didn't come out until it was quiet. He was embarrassed, but he admitted that he hid. And he showed us those positions where those shells fell. And what do we hear from Witness Nesic? He corroborates it at 8168 and talks about those few shells that landed on Djakovica. Finally, Witness B tells us that Nesic was in a bad mood and said something to the extent raze the whole town. Witness Negodic talks about an interception between a soldier and a commander, and the commander starts swearing, appears to be in a bad mood because he's swearing and says: Anything in the Old Town is a target. Negodic corroborates Witness B. All of these corroborative facts say that Witness B testified truthfully and should be believed by this Chamber. The Prosecution submits that none of the alleged military targets in the Old Town ever existed and that any such testimony of these three Defence witnesses should be rejected. And this all relates to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This all relates to the 6th of December. Where were the Croat positions? In our brief, in our map in the addendum in the co-addendum, we describe the positions. There are several and I don't feel there's a need to go into every single one. However, there's a difference as to four or five locations. Defence Witness Nesic places mortars by the Excelsior hotel, Bogisica Park, north of the Old Town on a vehicle nicknamed Charlie, by the Libertas Hotel, and finally, an artillery piece at the Lovrijenac Park. Witness Negodic disagrees and does not place mortars or artillery at any of those positions. He does place a rocket firing weapon at the Libertas hotel, but no mortars there. And in this conflict we suggest that Negodic should be believed. Why? Negodic was in the best position to explain and tell where his mortars and his artillery were located. No other witness made observations of mortars at the Excelsior Hotel, Bogisica Park, this Charlie vehicle running north of the Old Town, or the artillery piece at Lovrijenac park on December 6. No other Defence witness mentions these. Also, Nesic's inclusion of these in his ammunition expenditure report are fraudulent. As we've already said his claims to have fired at these locations just could not have occurred. Also, looking at these two persons, who has the motive to lie? We suggest Negodic has no motive to lie. He came in here. He described a large number of positions of his Croatian artillery or mortars. He described where they were located, when they switched, the amounts of ammunition that were used. Nesic, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond however, has to justify his actions. Based on witness testimony, they were firing on non-military targets. Nesic, as this Trial Chamber knows, is a potential war-crimes suspect. Therefore we submit that Negodic's testimony should be credited on the issue of Croatian military position. And we suggest that the mortars and the artillery positions were not located at those positions, at the Bogisica and Lovrijenac Park, or the mobile mortar known as Charlie was not moving just north of the Old Town on that date, December 6. So now we come down to the last issue. Who shelled the Old Town of Dubrovnik on December 6th? Witnesses Jokic, Negodic and Witness B say it was the JNA. Defence witnesses Tomislav Jovanovic, Drljan, Djurisic, and Pepic also saw or heard that the JNA weapons shelled the Old Town. The Defence's expert witness, Professor Vilicic, claims that the Old Town's damage was consistent with over 130 mortar shells from three JNA mortar batteries landing in the Old Town. These mortar batteries, we submit, were all under the command and control of the 2nd Operational Group. Colonel Poje, by a process of deduction or elimination, found the mortars within the 2nd Operational Group command shelled the Old Town. Now, if we look at paragraph 374 at page 77 of the Defence brief, they also place blame for the shelling of the Old Town on the JNA. If I read the last sentence: "Accordingly, Defence concludes beyond any doubt," -- not beyond a reasonable doubt -- it says "beyond any doubt that all alleged damages that might have been inflicted to the Old Town of Dubrovnik could have been accused exclusively by the use of artillery and mortars, the use of which was authorised by Admiral Jokic beyond any reasonable doubt." We agree that all damages to the Old Town on the 6th of December were caused exclusively by the JNA. We note that those JNA units that caused this damage were under the command and control of the 2nd Operational Group. We disagree, though, as to Admiral Jokic's role or acts as alleged in that paragraph. Therefore, we submit that the evidence has demonstrated beyond a reasonable doubt that the units under the command of the 2nd Operational Group, units under the command and control of the accused, Pavle Strugar, shelled the Old Town of Dubrovnik on the 6th of December. Attorney William Fenrick will now discuss the legal consequences of these facts, or if the Court would like to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the fundamental purpose of international humanitarian law is to reduce the net loss of innocent lives and injury to innocent people and damage to civilian objects in armed conflict. Essentially, international humanitarian law is a second-level barrier to barbarism; the first-level barrier is prevention of war itself. This case is of particular significance because it is one of the very few which purport to apply the general principles of international humanitarian law to combat activities. Law is most important when it's most fragile. Nowhere is it more important than when it attempts to impose limits on the violence of combat. There are virtually no precedents for the application of law to combat situations. We do have the Galic case here. Certainly if we look at the post-World War II war-crimes cases and other ones, nobody bothered about prosecuting the conduct --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Indeed, some people have on occasion indicated that this kind of case is simply non-justiciable. We would submit, however, that it is important to apply this body of law and to apply it correctly. Essentially, it's the submission of the Prosecution that we are not here to interpret the law for the JNA or interpret the law for the shelling of Dubrovnik; we are here to interpret the law and to apply the law for all armies everywhere. There is only one set of standards. These are the standards which must be applied here. The fundamental principle of international humanitarian law as it applies to combat situations is the principle of distinction, the obligation on parties to a conflict to distinguish between civilian populations and combatants and to distinguish between civilian objects and military objectives and to direct their military operations exclusively against military objectives. Military objectives are combatants, normally members of the armed forces, civilians taking a direct part in hostilities, and insofar as objects are concerned, objects which make an effective contribution to military action and whose destruction or neutralisation offers a definite military advantage. The Prosecution submits that none of the victims who are the subjects of counts 1, 2, and 3 of the indictment were either combatants or civilians taking a direct part in hostilities. All of them were civilians. The only one where one might query a bit as to the status of the victim is Mato Valjalo, a civilian driver for the Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik. The Defence has submitted that Mr. Valjalo should not be regarded as a civilian because of his employment of the time, as a driver for the Crisis Staff, and because he is presently in receipt of a pension as a disabled veteran as a result of injuries received during the shelling. The Prosecution submits that there is simply no indication that Mr. Valjalo meets the very rigid criteria of a civilian taking a direct part in hostilities. The real question is: Was he or was he not a member of the armed forces at the time when his injury occurred? Exhibits P60 and D24 indicate he was a civilian driver called up to perform service as such. He did, however, receive a pension as a disabled veteran. It's submitted this is not a persuasive indicator that he was a member of the armed forces at the time, basically, because receipt of such a pension appears to be completely unrelated to membership in the armed forces. We have the witness Negodic, the Croatian chief of artillery, who was in fact injured on the same date. He indicated in his testimony that he was in receipt of a civilian pension for injuries that he received. That's at page 5335. The Prosecution also submits that there were no military objectives in the Old Town of Dubrovnik on the 6th of December. The Prosecution certainly must admit that weapons positions are legitimate military objectives. But as argued by Mr. Weiner, we submit there were no such positions in the Old Town on the 6th of December, 1991.
