The Defence submits that the Old Town was filled with military objectives during the attack, including the Crisis Staff headquarters, centres in which information was gathered on JNA units, observation posts and members of the Croatian forces. Essentially, the Prosecution submits the Defence is trying to make something out of nothing. The Prosecution has already addressed the Crisis Staff headquarters issue in its brief, paragraphs 232 and 3. The fact -- if it is a fact -- that persons in the Old Town watched JNA vessels with binoculars or kept logs indicating vessel movements does not turn the location of these persons into military objectives. An attack on these positions or on these people would not confer a definite or indeed any military advantage. If, for the sake of argument, which the Prosecution certainly does not concede, it was considered there were military objectives in the Old Town, the Prosecution submits that these objectives would be of relatively little military significance, as an attack on them, particularly using the kinds of weapons which were used by the JNA on the 6th of December, mortars for the most part, would be bound to cause disproportionate loss or damage to civilians or civilian objects in comparison to the military advantage which could be derived from an attack on them. An attacker is simply not entitled to destroy all or a substantial portion of the Old Town in order to destroy an unimportant military objective. Further, as the Defence has suggested that the use by Croatian forces of mobile weapons such as truck-mounted mortars somehow placed an unfair burden on the JNA, it's submitted by the Prosecution that you take your military objectives as you find them. There are lots of mobile military objectives: Tanks, military aircraft. No one suggests that the tank has to stay still while you shoot at it. No one suggests that the aircraft must remain suspended in the air. In fact, the JNA used tanks itself during its attack on Srdj. No one would ever suggest that it's legally acceptable -- or for that matter that it makes military sense -- to launch an attack at a place where the tanks were two days before. There's no legal or military reason for adopting a different approach for truck-mounted mortars. The Prosecution submits that what one should look at when trying to determine the appropriate burden to be imposed on an attacking force are the standards set out in Additional Protocol 1. If one looks at Article 51.7 of Additional Protocol 1, there certainly is an obligation imposed on a defending force not to use the presence or movement of civilians to shield military objectives from an attack. Article 51.8, however, the following paragraph goes on to emphasise that a breach of its obligations by one party to a conflict simply does not release another party from its obligations with respect to civilians, in particular its obligations to take the appropriate precautionary measures. Even if -- which the Prosecution most certainly does not concede -- Croatian weapons were deployed in or close to the Old Town, the JNA was still obligated to comply with the principle of proportionality and to take all practicable measures to minimise civilian casualties. The Defence has also argued in paragraphs 576 to 78 of its brief that Croatia has violated its obligations under The Hague Cultural Property Convention by placing military positions in the Old Town or too close to the Old Town or by moving military personnel through the streets of the Old Town. The Prosecution submits, concedes, that allowing soldiers in uniform and armed to wander through the Old Town, if such occurred, was certainly a foolish practice, but it certainly does not amount to using a centre for the movement of military personnel or materiel such that the Old Town should be deemed to be used for military purposes within the meaning of Article 8 of The Hague Cultural Property Convention. Further, the location of Croatian Defensive positions relatively close to the Old Town, if there were such, may be an unwise or imprudent practice, but it does not remove the Old Town or any of the buildings in it from the scope of Article 3(D) of the statute. The buildings remain as they were; they are institutions dedicated to religion or the various other purposes listed in Article 3(D). The Prosecution must observe that it has, in fact, charged the accused under Article 3(D) of the statute not with an unenumerated offence related to a violation of The Hague Cultural Property Convention or a violation of any other provision granting special status to the Old Town. The distance issue is, it is submitted, simply irrelevant to the status of the buildings as such. The Prosecution submits that the appropriate approach in cases where objects within the scope of Article 3(D) are located in proximity to military objectives is to apply the principle of proportionality. An object within the scope of Article 3(D) cannot be absolutely insulated from attack if an important military target is located adjacent to it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, the interpreters are having trouble keeping up with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder if you could take things a little more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I'll endeavour to do so, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: An object within the scope of Article 3D cannot be insulated from an attack if an important military attack is adjacent to it. If there was a tank factory or a large number of weapons, for example, located in the middle of the Old Town, those aren't military objectives. They may be attacked, subject to the application of the rule of proportionality. If damage caused by the attack does, however, cause disproportionate losses to civilians and civilian objects including objects within the scope of Article 3D, then the Prosecution submits Article 3D has been violated. The Prosecution would also submit that when buildings do have a special status which raises them beyond the category of civilian objects alone, then there should be -- and the Prosecution concedes it's difficult to determine exactly how one goes about calculating it -- but we would submit that it should have an additional value for the purposes of determining proportionality. The cornerstone of the crime base for the case against the accused is the unlawful attack charges, Counts 3 and 5 in the indictment. The mental element for both of these offenses is addressed in a corrigenda filed on the 7th of September by the Prosecution. We submit the mental element is willful, as discussed in paragraphs 214 and 214(A) of the Prosecution brief. That is the mental element includes both intention and recklessness, bearing in mind both the Galic trial decision and the Blaskic appeal decision. The Prosecution submits that if the meaning of recklessness must now be understood as acting with an awareness of the substantial likelihood that the offence will be committed, the Prosecution has established the mental element for the unlawful attack charges beyond a reasonable doubt. The physical element for unlawfully attacks is addressed particularly in 213 of the Prosecution brief which quotes from paragraph 56 of the Galic Trial Chamber decision. And for unlawful attacks, it's "acts of violence directed against the civilian population or individual civilians not taking part in hostilities causing serious death -- can't have too many serious deaths -- causing death or serious injury to the body or health of members of the civilian population." The Prosecution submits that the physical element for unlawful attacks on civilian objects is substantially similar. Further, whether or not an attack has been directed against civilians or civilian objects is an evidentiary question, which involves an assessment of among other things the results of the attack; the surrounding circumstances including the presence of nearby military objectives; and the state of mind of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speaker please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You began to speed up with your enthusiasm for your subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you need to take a big breath after every sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I'll endeavour to do so, sir. The Prosecution also submits for reasons given in its brief at paragraphs 215 and 218 that indiscriminate attacks and disproportionate attacks may also be regarded as direct attacks on civilians or civil objects. The main thrust of the Prosecution argument is that the attack on the Old Town was intentional; that the civilian losses and the damage caused the buildings was not an indirect or collateral result of shell fire directed at alleged military objectives in the Old Town or close by. Although the principle of proportionality was addressed at some length in the Prosecution brief, it must be addressed further because of arguments raised in the Defence, brief particularly in 567 to 570 and in particular at paragraphs 573 to 580. If we take a look at the origins of the concept of proportionality, I suggest it's inextricably linked to the principle of distinction. You don't really have any treaty which as explicitly addresses -- or, for that matter, implicitly -- addresses the principle of proportionality, until the development of the additional protocols. In additional protocol 1, in particular, in a number of articles, 55.5B, 57.2A and 57.2B and in addition, 85.3B, there are references to excessive. The word "proportionality" is not used. That being said, the concept "excessive" clearly is an implicit reference to proportionality. There's a slightly different statement of the proportionality concept in the statute of the International Criminal Court. That statute uses the expression "clearly excessive," rather than merely excessive or rather than excessive, as used in the additional protocols. The words are there. The application of the words is not as clear as we would like it to be. The concept of proportionality or the application of the concept raises a number of issues for us. One of them is: Who is or who should be the decision-making concerning the application of the principle of proportionality? If we look at paragraph 58 of the Galic Trial Chamber decision, it submits that the decision-maker should be a reasonably well-informed person in the circumstances of the actual perpetrator making reasonable use of information available. And that person has to determine whether or not he could - he or she - could expect excessive civilian casualties to result from an attack. The next issue is perhaps a more difficult one: What is that we are comparing? Because we certainly seem to have a number of suggestions made by both various Defence witnesses and also in the Defence brief. The Prosecution submits that what we compare is, in fact, very clearly set out: We are comparing concrete and direct military advantage anticipated with the anticipated incidental loss of civilian life, injury to civilians, damage to civilian objects, or a combination thereof. We aren't comparing whether or not one side has more weapons than the other, whether or not one side has better weapons than the other, whether or not one side suffers more combatant casualties than the other. The Defence has suggested in paragraph 568 of its brief that if five JNA soldiers were killed and several wounded by Croatian fire on the 6th of December and only two civilians were killed and two injured in the Old Town, that's not disproportionate. Well, whether that measure is disproportionate or not, it's simply irrelevant to assessing proportionality for our purposes where we're comparing military advantage versus civilian losses. It should be observed that the one practical or the one actual judicial application of the principle of proportionality is, in fact, in the Galic case, the discussion of the Dobrinja football game incident at paragraphs 372 to 387 and in particular paragraph 387. If one looks, however, at the discussion of the Dobrinja football game, which was an incident where Bosnian Serb forces shelled a football or soccer game and caused slightly more military casualties than civilian casualties, the Court in that case finessed the requirement to decide whether or not causing slightly more military casualties than civilian casualties was proportionate or disproportionate, because what it did was focus on the intention of the attacking force. And the approach taken was that if what was shelled was a soccer game, you could expect that there would in fact be a substantial crowd of civilians there. There may be other people, too, but the bottom line was: What was in the mind of the decision-makers launching the attack? And the Court was of the view that as long as the -- one could conclude that the mental element or the expectation of the attacker was that one would be causing a large number or a disproportionate number of civilian casualties and then in the end result, what you had was -- were some civilian casualties, you didn't have to total up the scores. You didn't have to say: Well, there are more military than civilian, therefore it's not disproportionate or it's proportionate. The Prosecution would submit in this case the same sort of approach is perhaps particularly appropriate. Here what we have is the shelling of a populated city with a significant number of civilians. Whether or not you in fact had a relatively small number of civilians killed or injured during the attack is not quite as relevant as what one could presume was the intention of the people directing the attack in the first place. If they are firing shells on a populated city or a populated area, they can expect to cause a significant number of civilian casualties. In fact, if one looks at Dubrovnik, if one is launching shells at the Old Town that is basically all you can expect to cause, civilian casualties. You can't expect that launching shells or firing shells into the Old Town is going to result in substantial military casualties. PARKER: If one, Mr. Fenrick, is attempting to apply a principle of proportionality or is looking at what is excessive in this context, surely counting the dead, military versus civilian, can't be a suitable test, given the relative uncertainty in armed conflict of those who may be killed, those who may be injured, those who by some miracle or another escaped such consequences. Would it not perhaps be more to the point to be seeking to compare the military objective against the loss of civilians and civilian property, rather than head counts on each side?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: We would agree very much, Your Honour. It's never going to be simply a question of head count, if for no better reason that you're comparing entirely unlike quantities or values. How can one make a head count if, for example, you destroy a tank and wound a child beside the tank? The head count factor is very difficult to apply, but it's got to be, presumably, some kind of an estimate of the military advantage considered -- taking all factors into account, more than simply counting heads. And indeed, some heads would be much more -- or would be regarded, even from a purely military value, of much greater value than others. For example, if one takes a look at what happened in the recent war in Iraq, certainly the American forces made repeated attempts to hit Saddam Hussein and attack a number of locations where he was. In fact, he wasn't at any of those locations or it doesn't appear he was. Presumably in that case if one in fact had reliable intelligence which didn't seem to be applicable in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's rare in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Very much so, and particularly so in those types of attacks. I think you can make -- if one is attacking in an area like the or around an area like the Old Town, with the intensity of the conflict as it was -- in other words, not a conflict where a great deal of combat is doing going on. We're not talking Stalingrad here, we're talking about essentially a small-unit attack with a degree of covering fire. And one would submit in this particular case, in fact you can make a reasonable guesstimate ahead of time as to whether or not you are likely to be causing disproportionate civilian casualties. It's not an easy exercise, there's no question about it. But one would submit that shelling from Zarkovica, for example, where you can see what you're firing at and firing from a number of the other areas, one could make a reasonably realistic estimate. When you're talking ground warfare, you're not talking about the kind of decision-making process that you normally would have when you're talking about aerial attacks, for example, where it's practical to plan something and make sophisticated computer models and try to make a pretty precise estimate, or an outer-range estimate, of whether or not something is likely to cause a number of civilian casualties. It's more difficult to do it in a ground warfare situation. But in an extreme ground warfare situation, and by extreme, not that the intensity of the conflict was extreme, but what we're talking about is a situation where you have an extreme ability, a much greater degree of opportunity to try and calculate potential losses, I think it's quite manageable to make a reasonably realistic estimate of what the civilian casualties would be in connection with the attack on Dubrovnik on the 6th of December. It's just a different kind of fighting in a way. Now, if I might move on. One of the other questions which the Defence raised in connection with proportionality was the question of scale. And in fact, they quoted Canadian Forces Law of Armed Conflict manual. And in there they paid particular attention to a provision which says: "In deciding whether the principle of proportionality is being respected, the standard of measurement is the anticipated contribution to the military purpose of an attack or operation, considered as a whole." Now, the Canadian manual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But that's only referring to one side. If it's proportional, you've got to have two sides, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Well, I think -- well, you're -- the quotes "operation as a whole," presumably would mean extended military operation where what you would be trying to do is calculate your military advantage versus the anticipated civilian losses during that period of time. I think it would be something -- I think it would be two-sided, Your Honour, but it would be something where you have a more of a macro type of application rather than micro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can [Realtime transcript read in error: "can't"] see the sense of putting on the one scale the military objective and the significance of that and on the other hand or on the other scale the foreseeable - to a person in the position of the decision-maker, the foreseeable to civilians and civilian probably. I can see that as having some sense in this context. But you've got to be comparing the two sides for something to be proportional.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: You have to be comparing. Whether military advantage is interpreted in terms of you are receiving -- you are having casualties inflicted on your own force or whether you're talking about inflicting casualties on the other force -- -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or gaining a position --

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Unquestionably. But I submit the particular revision which the Defence refers to is something which is in fact addressed in our brief in paragraphs 222 to 224. And what you've got are a number of countries, of which Canada is one, and the Canadian statement is referred to in our brief, which says or which certainly can be read to say that when you're trying to determine whether or not something is -- whether or not what you've got is a disproportionate end result, you would look not simply at an attack directed against one military objective but at an attack directed against a range of military objectives in the course of some kind of an operation. And that is certainly both a defensible interpretation of the additional protocols and their provisions dealing with the principle of proportionality, and certainly in accord with the statements of interpretation of a number of countries that ratified the additional protocols. That being said, however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I just interrupt you before it goes off the screen. I see at 62, probably 37 -- I was saying I could see and it's come out as "I can't see." We'll just note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: The Prosecution in this particular case submits that it's defensible and quite acceptable to adopt a scale for determining proportionality essentially on a military objective by military objective basis, that there is no need in our case to adopt a more global approach. And we have a number of reasons for submitting that. One is we certainly are not in this particular case engaged in prosecuting the grave breach of disproportionate attack which may or may not, because of the surrounding words in the additional protocols, require us to adopt a more global approach. Another reason for adopting the more tactical approach is that we are here -- first it was adopted -- it was adopted in the Galic case. Secondly, it is in fact an approach which is commonly adopted elsewhere. If one looks, for example, and there are references in the brief to the Amnesty International study of the Yugoslav bombing campaign, certainly there the entire dialogue is framed in terms of whether or not an attack on a particular military objective is proportionate or disproportionate. There are similar reports by Human Rights Watch. And in fact if one looks at the other reference which is in the brief to the approach taken by the American government during I think it was the Kosovo bombing campaign, their approach once again is that they attempted to assess the likelihood of collateral casualties on a military objective by a military objective basis. And perhaps as another argument or another two arguments in support of that type of an approach, one is we are not in this case trying to argue that the end result of the attack -- that it's possible to have something which is both disproportionate and yet not at the same time in substance an attack directed against the civilian population. We are not arguing for some kind of a lower standard, that somehow or other that you could conclude an attack was disproportionate but it wasn't in substance directed at civilians. And also in a way we would submit that this is an evidentiary standard that we're talking about. It's something from which one could conclude in substance that what you do have is an attack directed against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When one is looking at a military objective, the approach of looking at one particular target, then distinctly and separately at another target when there have been successive attacks may be appropriate I would think in some factual situations, but if it was part of a significantly bigger campaign, a planned campaign, that had an overall objective of which these individual targets were but a part, would it not be appropriate also to have regard to the bigger picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: We submit it's entirely appropriate to have regard to the bigger picture, Your Honour, but it can still -- the assessment can still be carried out by a military objective, on a military objective basis. If I can use an entirely different example. Let's suppose we've got four bridges across a river and the object is to try and keep the forces from one side from reinforcing by sending troops across the bridge. It may well be that one derives substantially greater benefit from taking out the fourth bridge after you've knocked the other three down than you do from knocking the first three. The context is relevant, but you're still, we would submit, trying to determine proportionality. It's still practical to say, okay, there's only one bridge left. When we determine the military advantage from striking that particular bridge it becomes -- we get a much greater military advantage out of neutralising the fourth bridge than we did out of attacking the other three. But that's still something which can be done on an objective-by-objective basis. But yes, context is relevant. If I might move away from proportionality, Your Honour. Even the Defence appears to have concluded that Croatian forces did not shell the Old Town on the 6th of December. Logically, since no one else is available, the shelling must have been done by the JNA. There are, one would submit, only three options practicable. One is they attacked the Old Town as an act of revenge or mindless military vandalism. The other is they attacked military objectives which they thought were in the Old Town. And the third is that what they were doing was attacking objectives near to the Old Town and what you had was some kind of collateral effect spreading over. The Prosecution submits that we have already addressed adequately the situation in the Old Town under either the mindless vandalism or they were striking at military objectives point of view. What we would like to do is address the issue of attacking objectives which were near to the Old Town and causing collateral damage. We've got two different approaches taken by the expert witnesses. If one looks at the approach taken by Colonel Poje for the Prosecution, one would be inclined to conclude that it was very unlikely that shell fire directed at military objectives would -- outside the Old Town would have in fact landed in the Old Town. If, on the other hand, one accepts the approach of Dr. Vilicic, it would appear that collateral damage to the Old Town while attacking military objectives close to the Old Town would be more likely. The Prosecution submits, however, that if one looks at the Prosecution brief, the Defence appears to believe that simply asserting that civilian losses or damage to civilian objects constitute collateral damage as a defence. That's simply wrong. They've still got to assess the proportionality factor, and that clearly has not been done. It's our submission that if one does -- first of all, the conclusion which would be derived is that the damage was disproportionate. And secondly, in fact, when one bears in mind the kind of weapons and the tactics used by the Defence, in fact they made no efforts to minimise civilian casualties. My apologies. The JNA made no effort to minimise or reduce collateral casualties. They used mortars, which are aerial weapons. The 120-millimetre mortar projectile has an effective zone within which it might cause death or injury of 60 metres. And the weapon itself, the projectiles from a mortar, although it might be the weapon of choice in some urban warfare situations, is one which doesn't hit exactly what it is aimed at. In fact, if one looks at the testimony of Colonel Poje at page 6306, he points out -- or rather, in response to a question by the Defence, he indicated that if one was firing 120-millimetre projectiles at a platoon of mortars, hypothetically, if one looked at the weapon expenditure tables, it would take something like 2.160 rounds of 120-millimetre projectiles to have a 90 or an 80 per cent chance of neutralising the platoon of mortars. This would, of course, raise the question what happened to the other 2 thousand and some mortar shells which didn't hit the mortar platoon. Presumably they went somewhere, too, and one would be inclined to think that they could very well have caused civilian casualties or damage to civilian objects. Further, in addition to the choice of weapons, there was the technique of weapons. We had Colonel Poje testifying that if one wanted to attack a military objective which was located close to a sensitive area such as the Old Town, there were in fact techniques for doing that. And essentially, instead of the more military approach of firing a round over and firing a round under and trying to bracket and trying to hit the objective, what you could do is aim off to the side to a known objective and use that as your aim point and march towards the place where the objective was. If one takes a look at annex 4 in the Prosecution closing brief, one submits it's quite clear that if you look at the pattern of distribution, at least as indicated on that particular annex, there doesn't appear to have been a significant effort to try and focus. If there was an attempt to hit military objectives outside the Old Town, one would expect that a concentration of shells were landing close to the walls rather than being throughout the city. And that clearly is not what we have here. That concludes the part of my presentation which has to do with unlawful attacks, Your Honour. If I may for just a second consult. If I may close on this particular part dealing with unlawful attacks, Your Honour. My colleague has indicated I may not have been as clear as I should have been on some points. Our submission in connection with Mr. Valjalo is he was not a civilian taking part in direct hostilities. And secondly, although I mentioned in passing, the International Criminal Court definition of proportionality or their proportionality of offence which refers to clearly excessive, we are not supporting in any way or saying that that definition or those two words are applicable here. We are relying entirely on the language of the additional protocols which simply uses the word "excessive."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you move on, if you've finished those matters, on the hypothesis that you were putting to us that JNA that day may have been directing mortar fire at military targets close to but outside the Old Town, thus firing wide of the intended target, you were putting submissions critical of the choice of weapon by the JNA. What weapons other than mortars would you suggest they might have used?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: The weapons which they had, Your Honour, we understand to be Maljutkas, the 82-millimetre recoilless cannons. Both of those were, in fact, much more accurate or at least potentially much more accurate in the hands of capable users than the mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But range is a consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, but not so much for the Maljutka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It depends whether there's a pinpointed target or merely a potential target area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have had much evidence that they may have been aiming at mortar positions hidden in parks or in tennis courts that were out of view. A Maljutka is a line-of-sight weapon. If you can't see what you're aiming at you must have another weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the submission of the Prosecution is -- mortars are an appropriate weapon in a range of circumstances. But if the mortars are going to be used and are going to be fired against Croatian positions which are located relatively close to the Old Town, if there is nothing else available, nothing else in range, then our submission would be that there should be two considerations. One is that there is this technique for approaching a military objective or firing at a military objective which is close to something like the Old Town, which it doesn't appear was used. Secondly, whoever is engaged in providing the fire support should, we would submit, be taking proportionality into account. If, to use the example that I did use before, it took several hundreds of rounds from a mortar to neutralised another object, perhaps another mortar, and that other mortar was close to the Old Town, whoever is doing the firing can't simply ignore the requirement to go through the proportionality equation. He can't sit there and say: I have got to take out that military objective. What he's got to say is: If an attack aimed at that objective is, and according to my best estimate, something which is proportionate, then I can fire at it, then I should fire at it. If you can't, if it's going to be something where you lob hundreds of shells in a hope that you may actually hit a military objective, sometimes you just don't shoot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to delay you longer on that issue, then, Mr. Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I'm eating into my colleague's time here. The only other points I wanted to raise, Your Honour, is first of all you will note in our submission we did refer to international armed conflict. The Defence submitted in paragraph 619 that there is no need at all for the Tribunal to or for the Chamber to address the issue of international armed conflict. Our approach is perhaps out of an abundance of caution. We argue that all of the offenses which are charged are in fact ones that can be committed in either an international or internal armed conflict. Having said that, we are neither a Trial Chamber nor an Appeals Chamber. And for that reason, perhaps out of an abundance of caution, it might be appropriate -- it's appropriate for us to suggest that the international armed conflict issue is one for which we have introduced a substantial amount of evidence, and it would be our view that as a simple matter of fact the conflict by the date, by the 6th December, 1991, was an international armed conflict. The last comments that I shall make are extremely brief and understandably so. They have to do with modes of liability. We would submit that we have already addressed the modes of liability adequately in our brief, with the exception perhaps of Article 7.3, Command Responsibility. And of course there has been some jurisprudence fairly recently. We have the -- of course the standard criteria for command responsibility are that we must establish the existence of a superior-subordinate relationship; we must establish the superior knew that the criminal act or was about to be or had been committed; and we have to establish that the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the criminal act or punish the perpetrator thereof. We would submit that a key issue which must be established is the existence of a superior-subordinate relationship. The basic criteria for that are set out in the Celebici trial decision, which was blessed subsequently by the Appeals Chamber. And in paragraph 378 of the Trial Chamber decision it says: "In order for the principle of superior responsibility to be applicable, it is necessary that the superior have effective control over the persons committing the underlying violations of international humanitarian law in the sense of having the material ability to prevent and punish the commission of those offenses." In connection with that we would submit that whether or not effective control exists is essentially a question of fact; that in fact the effective control can exist or can be determined on the basis of an assessment of both de jure and de facto responsibility. The one point that has been made or was discussed in the Blaskic decision was whether or not one must establish that a person in effective control gave orders and those orders were obeyed. We would certainly suggest that the ability to give orders is an essential component of effective control, but having said that, it's certainly not the only one. We would certainly say that there is no way on earth in which the accused or anyone can say: I gave a general directive that the law of war is to be complied with. My subordinates did not comply with the law of war, therefore I didn't have effective control. That kind of argument is, we would submit, absurd. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fenrick. I think this is a convenient time for the next break. We will resume at quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I may just, as a follow-up point to something Mr. Fenrick spoke of. It is the submission of the Prosecution that on the 6th of December there was no military advantage in taking Srdj. The campaign in Dubrovnik was effectively to be at an end by virtue of the context that has been shown to this Chamber through the evidence of Mr. Rudolf and of Admiral Jokic, that the purpose of the exercise on the 5th and the 6th of December was to be comprehensive negotiations under the wing spread of the international community and Croatia and the SFRY, the JNA, to effect a withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia. It is inconsistent entirely to have any military campaign in this context. Secondly, in view of the fact that there was fighting that had broken out, it is equally the position of the Prosecution that the fire from the JNA that ensued was not protective cover fire but a continuation of aggressive targeting, and if in fact any protective fire were to have been authorised it would have been only that which was required to bring everything to an end. The parties should have negotiated immediately to stop hostilities, and restraint, which was addressed by General Zorc, would under these circumstances have been the option to have been exercised by the 2nd Operational Group command. It was not. Further -- I believe there may have been some reference this morning but I want to make sure that the Chamber is aware of it, that Ivan Negodic the chief of artillery for the Croatian defence, had addressed a comment overhead in an intercept to the effect of: "Commander, what can we hit in the town?" "Anything is a target." An absolute, overt violation of the principle of distinction. I draw the Chamber's attention to one of the most grotesque examples of a failure to adhere to adhere to the principle distinction which was brought out in the testimony of Novica Nesic, the commander of the anti-armour company among the accused's forces. The question was: "We did not monitor civilians moving about. Our job was to notice military targets moving about. After all, civilians were moving about Dubrovnik in the Old Town on a daily basis. Therefore, we did observe them moving about, but they were not of relevance to us." Transcript 8227. "We noticed people there on a daily basis, even more massive gatherings in the Old Town, and not small groups like this one. But then again, this was of no relevance to us." Novica Nesic, transcript 8228. "Civilians were moving about the Old Town and the Stradun on a daily basis and this was observed every day. This was of no military relevance to us, people walking about in the Old Town. We didn't record data on that because that was not important. None of those people put us at risk. Why would I be paying attention to a handful of civilians moving about a street and going about their business?" Novica Nesic, transcript 8229. So much for the implementation of the principle of distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't see the point of those comments, directed as you say to the principle of distinction between military and civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic suggested that the risk to be considered was the risk to the JNA troops by the civilians, that is consideration of what the civilians were doing was not foremost in their minds. This is how we have construed the evidence and that there was no consideration whatsoever about their being there. The general alert if someone were on the street in the face of a general alert, then that was that person's problem. It simply indicates that the purpose behind the concept was simply not drummed home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think in that answer you were bringing together more than one piece of evidence about more than one situation. But on the comments from the evidence of Mr. Nesic, I see now factually what you're saying those comments indicate. They may be understood, though, to illustrate something quite differently, that is that a military observation post is observing military actions in Dubrovnik and was not concerned with what the civilians were doing in their ordinary daily life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Our submission, Your Honour, is that monitoring the civilians becomes a critical point in determining what one does with one's military assets. And we have determined that to mean that was not factored into decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The existence of a superior-subordinate relationship, as was indicated, is one of the fundamental elements in determining 7.3 liability. And in discussing generally, rather, the accused's role in terms of all the units of the 2nd Operational Group. At all times material to the indictment, the accused was in a superior-subordinate relationship over those responsible for the unlawful attack on the Old Town. The 9th VPS and the 472nd MTBR, the brigade and elements thereof, were among the formations that were at all times relevant to the indictment subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group for operational purposes. In response to some of the assertions in the Defence brief, the general staff was the level at which the strategic -- concept of strategic would be applicable, not the operational level. General Zorc's testimony, I suggest, would be of great help in looking at the distinctions which were drawn in the course of the Prosecution's evidence. But the general staff provided the general objectives at the strategic level for the operation in Dubrovnik, while tactical decisions such as deployment of units, changes to subordination of units, issuing of combat orders, et cetera, were made at the level of the operational command, that is 2nd Operational Group commanded by the accused Pavle Strugar. In fact --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Prosecutor, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. In fact the Chamber has been presented and has heard evidence that the commander of the 2nd Operational Group issued combat orders. I need only to refer you to P119 and P121. Also D47 [Realtime transcript read in error: "27"] is an order which covers a span of issues which include maritime concerns. If I can ask for correction to D47. Note that the 472nd Brigade, the Trebinje Brigade, was a unique brigade in that it was viewed as a strike force. It was a formation that could address very specific needs for the purposes of a 2nd Operational Group and was manned accordingly and of course was outfitted with materiel accordingly. We remind the Chamber that the territorial borders drawn in maps D41 and D42 had no impact or relevance to the operations of a 2nd Operational Group in the Dubrovnik theatre. Taking a brief look at the 472nd Motorised Brigade: The General Staff singled out this brigade and subordinated it directly at the beginning of the Dubrovnik operations to the 2nd Operational Group, up on par with corps-level formations. The brigade had four battalions. The battalions were equipped with 82-millimetre-mortar recoilless guns, hand-held launchers, rocket launchers, Maljutkas, et cetera, and I turn the attention of the Chamber to 3840 so that it has an idea of what was in every battalion. There has been evidence presented to this Chamber that the use of weapons by the battalion as a whole was often outside of what was strictly a military necessity and outside of combat operations. I refer the Chamber to the testimony of Admiral Jokic, transcript 3869 and 70. I remind the Chamber that the arrival of Captain Kovacevic as a commander heralded the increase of a state of indiscipline in the battalion. That is T3856. Expert Witness General Zorc testified that the documents -- based on the documents that he examined, they were completely sufficient for him to conclude that the commander of the 2nd Operational Group had exclusive authority for implementing the tasks conferred upon him. He had all the necessary competence to command all units subordinated to his Operational Group, under transcript 6704 and 05. Also Exhibit D44 shows that the 2nd Operational Group was a broad-cast group, not only Dubrovnik. There has been a great deal of discussion throughout the trial about what has been referred to as a dual chain of command. The Prosecution submits there was no dual chain of command with respect to the 9th VPS, that the 9th VPS was at all times relevant to this indictment, subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group for operational purposes; that any links that were retained with the KVPO were administrative, and that it would be inconceivable that any other parent -- any other formation, superior formation, could have competed to give combat, operational orders to the 9th VPS, which was clearly, overwhelmingly from the evidence, subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group commanded at the time relevant by the accused, General Strugar. The issues that touch on activity or concerns of the VPO have dealt with supply, boats; I believe even there are a couple mentions in D96 which I can assist you with, if it would help to direct your attention. Page 64 of D96, an entry at 1441 hours with regard to resubordination of units belonging to the 9th VPS and the fleet commander's comment that he is unaware of the consent of the VPO given to the VPS to use fleet ships. Such was the nature of the relationship; nothing more. There was an intact chain of command structured according to the rules governing structuring of a command staff. The 2nd Operational Group had the fundamental organs that enabled it to control combat operations. Whether or not it employed them was a command decision by the accused, but they were there to be employed. The Prosecution submits that its evidence has established beyond and to the exclusion of every reasonable doubt that the accused, General Strugar, was the de jure commander of the forces of the 2OG and de facto the evidence is such that he exercised those reins of command to have his orders which were issued were carried out when he chose to have them carried out, and when they didn't he turned a blind eye. Again the turning of a blind eye, the selective enforcement of orders, is by no way a lack of effective control. It is irresponsible command, and in this instance it is criminal command. I cite you to Celebici appeal judgement paragraphs 192 and 256, Your Honours. There is clear evidence that the concept of singular, unified command in the JNA was the rule and it, in fact, was observed in the context of the facts surrounding our indictment. In the context of the centralised or orders-driven command system of the JNA, there was no room for parallel chains of command within the 2OG or for units to act outside the authority of the command of the 2OG. We cite to both Admiral Jokic's testimony, 3911, General Zorc, 6434 and 6594. Singleness of command meant there was only one commanding officer in an operational group. The Operational Group commander was the only one who issued orders related to the operations of the units of the operational group. The various relationships between and among command officers within the 2nd Operational Group -- and that would include, for example, officers such as Admiral Jokic who as the head of the 9th VPS was subordinated to General Strugar, and other officers reflect a wide spectrum of attitudes toward the campaign -- The Prosecution submits that those attitudes became eminently clear on the 6th of December. There has been a fair amount of evidence that, the Prosecution suggests, indicates that although lip service may have been paid by the accused to carrying out the order from Belgrade for a peaceful resolution to the Dubrovnik situation, in fact, his actions and attitude which were part of his command climate were to be contrary. The retention as his liaison officer and front-line contact with internationals and the cross-examinations of Colonel Sikimic very much indicated that irrespective of their views -- and Sikimic was deemed by the internationals to be someone who could not and should not be holding that position -- the retention of such a person suggests that the accused had no regard for how the other side would accept or not accept the proposals of the 2nd Operational Group. Further, in terms of real intent to bring about peace, the alleged or the so-called 11-point Ultimatum in October 1991 included conditions which were calculated never to be accepted. So the good faith, the bona fides of this type of alleged resolution was nothing more than lip service. It is the submission of the Prosecution that the accused sought a military solution as opposed to a peaceful solution to the crisis that was created in the Dubrovnik theatre. Looking, however, at another commander, Admiral Jokic, the Prosecution submits that his conduct and attitude, as attested to by Prosecution witnesses such as Davorin Rudolf, was one that was calculated to effect the intention from a strategic level to bring about the peaceful solution to the crisis, the military conflict and the attendant need to rebuild the infrastructure in Dubrovnik. He was, unfortunately, blocked in carrying this out by a number of factors within the 2nd Operational Group, the most significant of which, of course, was his superior commander, the accused. I will address the 2nd Operational Group commanding combat operations with a view of blockading Dubrovnik and issuing daily combat orders to its subordinate units including the 9th VPS and with regard to the daily tasks. The Prosecution submits that it would be sufficient to review carefully the terms of P119, P121 to see how clearly the accused had a hands-on, immediate, right up-front approach to running combat operations. And these of course included orders assigning specific tasks to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade, the very unit responsible for the shelling of the Old Town on the 6th of December, and the unit which on the 6th of December the accused knew to have been suspected of being responsible for shellings in November of the Old Town as well, and for which no punishment or investigation was meted out earlier. There has been an issue raised in the Defence brief about the alleged attempt by Admiral Jokic to lift the blockade on or about the 11th of November, suggesting that the VPO was in fact reigning over him as opposed to the 2nd Operational Group. This is a fallacy. We draw the Chamber's attention to the explanation which is very sound, presented by Defence Witness Drljan, who confirmed that the particular blockade, the control at issue there, was one that was passed by the United Nations Security Counsel Resolution. It had nothing to do --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. It was not the blockade that was imposed by the edict of D44 and does not offend the unified and singular chain of command on the 2nd Operational Group. The evidence establishes that combat orders were issued by the accused and then were followed with the very notable exception of orders instructing that attacks on the Old Town be prevented. We draw the Chamber's attention to the recent Blaskic appeals judgement as another example of effective control exercised by the commander. The Appeals Chamber went on to hold that the indicators of effective control are more a matter of evidence than of substantive law and those indicators are limited to showing that the accused had the power to prevent, punish, or initiate measures leading to proceedings against the alleged perpetrators where appropriate. I cite you to paragraph 69 of the Blaskic appeals judgement. It is clear from the evidence, Your Honours, that the accused did have at his disposal the organs necessary to mete out discipline when he chose to invoke them. There has been evidence that the murder of civilians in the Kiev Dolje [phoen] area was prosecuted in the military court of Sarajevo in January of 1992, having occurred in November of 1991 arising out of the area of the 2nd Operational Group which was the accused's area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution submits that an effective communication system enabled the accused to communicate with his subordinate units and that on the 6th of December there was communication between the accused and his subordinate commanders and personnel throughout the day, particularly in relation to the attack. We draw the Chamber's attention to Admiral Jokic's testimony on 4891 as well as the D96 diary which reflects messages to and from the 2nd Operational Group command, also concerning, for example, the need to put out fires. And there is certainly communication back and forth that supports the position. The evidence has shown that there was the material ability for the accused to discipline his subordinates. The accused, as is borne out by General Zorc at 6524, who stated that: "Even at the highest level of command is physically enable to visit the front according to doctrine, there would be no qualitative difference between what he knows and the actual ground because information flowed to him up the chain of command. There was indeed a functioning chain of command. If information was disregarded, that was a conscious decision of the command. It was not because it was the material ability to have a functioning chain of command and a flow of information. The accused's control over matters in the Dubrovnik theatre was all-encompassing and that extended to areas even such as civil affairs. I draw the Chamber's attention to the testimony of Defence witness Kurdulija, 7872; Cavtat town commander, who was from the 9th VPS directly subordinated to Colonel Pipovic; the assistant to General Strugar for civilian affairs was there until mid-December, 1991. Further, when the 2nd Operational unit groups entered Mokosica there was no fighting due to negotiations between the 2nd Operational Group command, representatives of the EU, Minister Kuchner and Admiral Jokic. I cite the testimony of Admiral Jokic at 4449 to 52. With respect to demilitarisation there were negotiations between the 2OG and the Crisis Staff several times between October to December. At times, the accused himself led negotiations and at times he set up a team led by Colonel Simicovic who proved to be someone who could not be dealt with by the international community. A point that the Prosecution wishes to drive home is that the accused passed off to his subordinate Admiral Jokic responsibilities to handle high-level contacts and undertakings with the international community. We draw the Chamber's attention to the Tivat meetings with the ambassadors and journalists on the 29th of October, 1991, where Ambassador Fietlaars confirmed that Belgrade told him you have a meeting with General Strugar "and presumably Admiral Jokic, and that in fact General Strugar made himself unavailable." We further draw the Chamber's attention to the most and more pertinent date of the December negotiations where Minister Rudolf confirmed that Zagreb through General Raseta and Belgrade indicated that he would be negotiating with General Strugar, and when he got to location, again, regrets sent but Admiral Jokic was given the job by General Strugar. We submit that the inference to be drawn from that is there was no wish to deal with internationals who were seeking either an explanation as to what was happening as a reaction to allegations of violations of international humanitarian law such as the mission of Ambassador Fietlaars, or to engage in a peaceful resolution of the conflict, as was the mission of Minister Rudolf. There has been suggestion on multiple occasions that because Admiral Brovit or General Kadijevic may have reached a step below the accused down to the Admiral, that that indicated that there was not the chain of command, the intact chain of command, and that the accused would consider himself out of the loop, basically pushed aside. That was put to rest, considered completely incorrect. To conclude that, by the testimony of General Zorc, 6624 and 25: "The federal secretary is in fact a superior in the chain of command and can thus ask from anybody from the top down in the chain of command for activities that he wants to see performed. And there was nothing unusual about General Kadijevic summoning General Strugar and Admiral Jokic on 6 December, albeit the subordinate-superior relationship between the two." As to exercising command on the 6th of December, interestingly, representing a change from the Prosecution's case where cross-examination of Prosecution Witness Colonel Colm Doyle the head of the monitoring mission for Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was in the accused's headquarters about midday on the 6th. The cross-examination during the case in chief led most to believe that there was a challenge to the fact of the meeting. In fact, the Defence case did a very quick reversal and confirmed the fact of the meeting, but then attempted to make Colonel Doyle, a very experienced person in the arena of negotiations in the former Yugoslavia, look like someone who couldn't follow and was not with the programme and completely misunderstood the accused's statement as relayed by Doyle that he had to open fire, he the accused had to open fire on Dubrovnik because his units had been fired at. The Prosecution submits there was no misunderstanding by Colonel Doyle, but in fact that this was related directly to the command the accused was exercising over units that day in Dubrovnik. It may have been a regrettable admission by the accused -- statement by the accused, rather -- accurate, and that the attempt to put Dr. Sikimic on to explain that away was laughable, given the explanation that the doctor tried to explain about his acrostic-style method of note-taking and suggestion that there was some misunderstanding, clearly, as to that issue the Chamber should reject wholly Dr. Sikimic testimony. It is system implausible and uncredible. The accused possessed the power to punish, to prevent, and to initiate measures leading to proceedings against perpetrators of the shelling of the Old Town at the time of the commission of the crime. He simply chose not to exercise those powers that were inherent in his command, in fact were his duty to exercise. Rather than going to the scene on the 6th of December, to going to the location where his units were firing and not obeying the orders to halt fire, he sat and wasted precious time -- Colonel Doyle, time that could have been used to prevent the horrific damage to the Old Town of Dubrovnik. It is very clear that units of the 2nd Operational Group did not honour the cease-fire that was in effect from approximately 13 November, and in fact disregarded the admonition about not undertaking any action with the major comprehensive cease-fire that was due to come into effect on the 6th of December. If the Chamber takes a look, this is in the brief, to the entries for the 5th of December, it is very clear that preparations were being made for the peace talks. The discussions about the Argosy being granted safe passage clearly indicates that the end of hostilities was contemplated and clearly indicates that, from Admiral Jokic's perspective, who has shown that he would not put internationals in harm's way, clearly Admiral Jokic fully intended to see that peace negotiation entered into, signed, and implemented. If the Chamber also takes a look at D96 for the entry for the 4th of December. Just to draw your attention to it, page 59, the entry is 7.50 hours. There is an reference also that Minister Rudolf, Ciric, and Kriste have sailed from Split at 7.05 heading for Dubrovnik, due to arrive around 1300, will remain in Dubrovnik. Clearly the 2OG was aware of the presence of these persons and in a rare moment of appropriate documentation, these entries are found in D96. I believe the Chamber even made the same observation that D96 that the war log is not a complete record, is not a total chronology, it does not contain everything that witnesses said that it should contain. It does however, contain those passages. Returning for a brief moment to the organs that were available to carry out investigations that were required in the event of breach of discipline. There was a suggestion that because of the confusion, the times, the breakups, the political situation, the movement from Split, that there was a shortage of military personnel and security organs. That is unacceptable and General Zorc has indicated that there is a duty to find them. That whether or not peace or war dominates, the criminal violations must be addressed. And I just ask the Chamber to review the testimony of General Zorc confirming that. I also draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that Colonel Djurisic, Gojko Djurisic, a Defence witness, testified that the 9th VPS has military police units and if a crime was committed within the units under his responsibility he would have taken measures to investigate and prosecute. Mr. Djurisic went on to state that the failure to take such measures would lead to the units repeating to the units relating such acts in the belief that it could be done with impunity. I cite transcript 6991 and 92. And of course Djurisic's formation, his unit was directly subordinate to the accused in the 2nd Operational Group. We note that evidence has presented, both in the form of documentary and testimonial, about various offenses which were addressed. In late December an order came out concerning prosecution of war booty. Admiral Jokic indicated he had yet to find any evidence of Prosecution for international humanitarian law violations concerning unlawful attacks. There was a frontal attack lodged against Witness Jokic by two Defence witnesses, Petre Handziev and Miroslav Javanovic, and the Prosecution wishes to address each witness. First Handziev. The picture painted by him was one of -- and by observing of a man who had a -- had something to pick against Admiral Jokic. Clearly there was extremely hard feeling there. Exceptional bias. And I draw the Chamber's attention to the comments by him about the Admiral being a renegade and that General Strugar, the accused, was a knight to whom Dubrovnik ought to erect a monument. I cite transcript 7657. The implausibility of the story that was woven by Mr. Handziev about a phone call is best attacked by way of background of the witness. The witness is a witness who came in on a mission. It is clear that he was out to discredit for personal reasons the Admiral. It is clear from the Admiral's rebuttal that this man could not have possibly been in a position to have heard what he purports to have heard and that in fact the entire conversation that Handziev testified to never took place. I draw the Chamber's attention to the lack of resoluteness of which Handziev spoke when confronted by the Prosecution on cross-examination with the assertion that in fact there was no conversation between General Kadijevic and Admiral Jokic where he said: "If that's the kind of information you have -- I'm telling you what I remember. If you have some kind of other information through some intelligence services, that's debatable, too. And that's the end of it." It is absolutely implausible that 13 years after an alleged event that took place, but arguendo, had it taken place, that a man whom the Chamber observed with the same acumen as the Prosecution, that he would recall the detail of grammar points of the Serbo-Croatian language which he claims were etched in his memory. Now, this is a man whose first language was Greek and then Bulgarian, then somewhere down the line B/C/S. It is simply implausible that etched in his memory might be the use of a particular pronoun in a conversation. The witness did, however, occasionally when caught off guard, give points that the Prosecution submits were truthful. He did confirm the arbitrariness of which events and which data were entered into the logs at operation centres. In fact, not everything that should have gone in went in. It was very much what the writer chose to put in. And that would be 7651, transcript. He also confirmed, more importantly, that he, Handziev, who sat at the operation centre at Kumbor was taken by surprise. He did not expect the hostilities of the 6th of December. Neither did Gojko Djurisic. Neither did Defence witness Novakovic. These are persons who if it were an operation of the 9th VPS would be absolutely calculated to know and it is absurd to suggest that persons in these positions would not. It is clear -- the Prosecution evidence is overwhelming -- that whoever, if anyone, in the 9th VPS had overtaken this, it was not Admiral Jokic. The behaviour of the Admiral just before and on that day indicates that he invested his personal and professional credit in advancing the strategic goals that he was ordered to advance, that is in effecting a comprehensive agreement with the highest level of the Croatian government -- we are talking about minister level, not the local level -- and did everything in his power to do so, reserving an issue to the accused on a point that was not insignificant but which the accused begged off again to the Admiral later. The amount of energy that the Admiral invested on the 6th, perhaps not in the right way and he has pled guilty. I emphasise the Admiral is not on trial. He has accepted his responsibility, he has been sentenced, and he will serve. He has told the Chamber what happened with no motive whatsoever to fudge, to expand, to spin. There's essentially no benefit to him. He's effectively, in that sense, got no dog in that fight. He has paid his dues there. And the attacks that were lodged had been attacks that we submit should be disregarded; that the ten-plus, eleven-plus days on the stand were such and under ruling cross-examination, he displayed his responses. He carried them out with dignity and with candor. As a human being he has lapses of memory and is entitled to such. But he was a candid witness who in no way attempted to discredit his one-time co-accused, General Strugar, the accused. I'd like to turn for a moment to Miroslav Jovanovic. The first point came as a bit of a surprise when the request for videolink, which in and of itself is not an extraordinary request, but the basis for it was allegedly frailty of spouse, ill health, unwillingness as long as such frailty persisted to leave his home in the former Yugoslavia. As it turns out it appears to have been a different reason. It appears that it was initially a fear of possible exposure, as was brought out during the course of argument, to his role in the operations of the 6th. And the Prosecution submits simply an act of pure cowardice, unwillingness to accept the face-to-face process that he would have had to accept and requested the buffer to attempt to shield what was a lengthy bit of testimony without any foundational merit. Miroslav Jovanovic was brought into the picture after the fact. It is unclear whether his own desire for vengeance against Admiral Jokic was the motivating factor, but it is clear from his evidence that he had hard feelings. His career was short-circuited as a result of the what he calls his removal. In fact, the Prosecution submits this is not the arena in which to vent that type of vendetta. The testimony that he gave was false testimony, the Prosecution submits. If the Chamber takes a look, for example, at the various bits of -- the various pieces of evidence about meetings. Defence Witness Lemal discussed Captain Kovacevic being at Ivanica on the 5th of December roughly at 1830 staying until 2000 or 2030 hours. There is certain corroboration by Nesic, referring to "early evening." Stojanovic also corroborates the time frame. But Miroslav Jovanovic alone puts Kovacevic at a meeting in Kupari from 1800 taking him to 1930 or 2000 hours the same day. It is impossible to be in two places at once. It is absolutely certain that Miroslav Jovanovic was not telling the truth. Three in Ivanica and one is putting him in Kupari. The Chamber itself can draw its conclusions, that that's not what happened. The notion of removal, the concept that was raised by the Defence in its brief was removing Jovanovic but inability to remove Kovacevic. The Prosecution submits these are different issues. Jovanovic was placed for a very brief period of time to substitute for Strikovic [phoen] who was permitted to go on leave because there was no activity contemplated for that period of time. He was in position approximately one day when he claims to have been brought into discussions at Kupari which the rebuttal evidence of Admiral Jokic indicates was not correct, that he did not attend. The removal of such a person was nothing more than putting him back to where he was before. What was clear from the evidence is that Admiral Jokic was unable to remove or otherwise act upon Captain Kovacevic, and the reason for that was because of the protective layer between his ability to do so and Kovacevic that was provided by the accused, General Strugar. There is no dispute that the documents suggest that at some point Admiral Jokic went along with the Kovacevic version of facts that General Strugar ordered him to go along with. The Admiral, as the realist, understood that there was nothing he could do. He has pled guilty; he has owned up to these things. The admiral talked about the 14th of December visit by General Panic and the Defence came in by some attempt to contradict by saying it was a March visit. They are not inconsistent. There is not an inconsistency there. I draw the Chamber's attention to the rebuttal testimony, the inclusion of the December visit, about which he is adamant and which makes sense indicates that there could also have been a separate visit in March of 1992. Excuse me just a minute, Your Honour, I'll try to collect the last on this issue. Prosecution will address also Gojko Djurisic. The Defence witness Djurisic denied receiving orders from Admiral Jokic. Jokic testified that on the 6th in the morning in the course of a phone conversation, he had requested Djurisic to go to Zarkovica and stop the attack. There's no contradiction between those two versions at all. The difference is as to who called whom and if the Admiral asked Djurisic or ordered him to go to Zarkovica to stop the attack. It is reasonable that there could have been a lapse in the Admiral's recollection of it. What is certain is that Djurisic confirmed the surprise, the anger and even swearing employed by the Admiral over the attack, that he had no understanding of how it could have happened, and Djurisic himself knew nothing about the attack. Mr. Djurisic confirmed conducting a phone conversation with the Admiral in the morning and that he confirms that the admiral sounded angry, asking who was shelling Dubrovnik when he was negotiating a cease-fire. I turn the Chamber's attention -- I'm sorry, I have to look for that particular cite, but it looks like transcript 4069 -- sorry, that's not correct. 4069. I'll correct it if I'm wrong. I also direct the attention of the Chamber that there is an entry in D96 that Chief of Staff Zec relays the order to cease-fire at 0740 hours on the 6th, the entry. Looking at why it is absolutely implausible that Admiral Jokic would have had any part whatsoever on ordering an attack on Srdj in the face of these very major strategic negotiations, we emphasise the efforts, the going to Cavtat, the meetings; the negotiation process itself; the relaying to his units and reporting about it. The fact that the negotiations themselves were documented in the defence D96, that it was well known throughout the international community; these are points that without a doubt confirm that Admiral Jokic was clearly on a path to peace on that date and had no participation whatsoever in any planning of an operation on a feature which he has described in his own testimony as one the taking of which would be calculated to implicate Dubrovnik and specifically the Old Town. The suggestion that the testimony about the early-morning hours of the story of an attack initiated by Croatian forces falls into place when one looks at the use, for example, of D96. That story does not appear in D96. Kozaric, the communications officer, undoubtedly was given some information to cover for what was to be a serious violation of a strategic order to implement peace. Admiral Jokic was clearly out of the loop on this and it makes perfect sense that a version like that would have been passed on and that he would have recounted exactly what he was told. That it did not get into the log is not surprising given how much did not get into the log and given the speed with which action has to be taken once the hostilities broke loose. What is absolutely clear from Defence witnesses is that all casualty taken by the 2OG soldiers, Captain Kovacevic's unit, occurred after the attack initiated by Captain Kovacevic's people, not before. There was no Croatian provocation. There's a reference in D96 to some sniper fire. It is de minimus. There is nothing that even approaches the type of horrific taking lethal casualties that was the version of Kovacevic, designed to throw those who did not favour that action offsent. The Prosecution has made its submissions about sentencing which I will not rehash. I will simply draw the Chamber's attention to our position that one must look at two commanders charged with similar but not identical charges arising out of the same events and distinguish very strongly the role, the conduct of Admiral Jokic and the conduct of the accused, General Strugar. After his plea of guilty in August of 2003, Admiral Jokic gave yet another interview and in fact substantially cooperated with the Prosecution. And that substantial cooperation, we submit, was perhaps one of the most helpful discussions of what and how the JNA thought that has yet come to light in this institution through any testimony. It was perhaps, besides being of great relevance to the case, generally of great relevance to the Tribunal. The Admiral has not tried to assign responsibility to others, in sharp contrast to what has been presented in the Defence case. There has been a level of remorse expressed by the Admiral on the date, not once but twice on the date and then immediately thereafter, that greatly merits a distinction. The accused, according to Admiral Jokic, did not favour, did not permit the issuance of an apology or a regret. The Admiral did it anyway, that day. And perhaps to get on the band wagon, gosh knows why, a day later according to Minister Rudolf, a similar type of admission of control over the units causing the shelling of the Old Town was made and was also a form of expression of regret. Those are two very different men with two very different attitudes. The Prosecution has set forth its position and the recommendation for sentencing if convicting on all counts, is irrespective of motive liability, 13 to 15 years. And that takes into consideration the very specific issues to the accused over which there has been much evidence. I'm talking about not just age but health. The Prosecution has tried to factor in everything. It has paid close attention to the testimony of the accused's wife and believes that should a conviction follow, that that would be appropriate. Now, in terms of what conviction may be entered, the Prosecution submits that there is evidence sufficient for a conviction of ordering. There is evidence sufficient for a conviction of aiding and abetting. And there is evidence sufficient, certainly beyond a reasonable doubt, for 7.3. The jurisprudence will require because they arise out of the same count that the Chamber elect, based on the mode that best characterised the type of liability of, should it make that finding. The Prosecution has through both testimonial and documentary evidence and through a process of rather strict cross-examination brought to light as much as is known about what really happened in Dubrovnik at that time. The Prosecution submits that it is one of the more mysterious cover-ups of the conflict, that the lack of action to punish, albeit having been promised from as high up as Brovit [phoen] as related by Ambassador Fietlaars, in fact never materialised. The Chamber has heard from witness after witness in the Defence that no one really was punished for what was an outrageous violation of international humanitarian law. And again, the amount of cover-up that followed the event, whether it was in the form of a deluded report on damage, whether it was the continuous denial of the fact of damage of shelling, the ostrich approach, we didn't hear it officially. Whatever the reasons are, this case has brought to light the seriousness of the cover-up, and only through this case have really facts ever surfaced that tell us anything about what really happened there. The Prosecution submits that it has proven beyond the exclusion of every reasonable doubt every count charged in the indictment, that the Trial Chamber has heard evidence from which it can convicting the accused of either orders or aiding and abetting or 7.3, the failure to prevent or punish. And again, because of time restrictions, the detail as to what could have been done to prevent is more specifically laid out in the brief. The only inference, the Prosecution submits, that can be available from all the evidence taken in its totality is that the accused is guilty of the crimes charged. Thank you very much. I believe that concludes. Thank you, Your Honours and Counsel.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, just one sentence as a question for the Trial Chamber. There are three different briefs by the Defence in connection with the different documents that were filed, some in July and some in August this year, including those marked for identification and those marked as rejoinder evidence as well as documents that the Defence wishes to have admitted as documentary evidence. Unfortunately the Defence team has not so far received any rulings from you pursuant to those filings which may be of relevance to our final position in this case. Therefore, the Defence would like to pose this one question: When and in what way will that be dealt with by the Trial Chamber? Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I do agree that you have not received those and that is unfortunate. Due to the break and other commitments, those decisions are not yet filed. Certainly you should proceed in your submissions on the assumption that the documents will be admitted. The decisions which are imminent, if they do not allow into evidence one or more of the documents, the Trial Chamber will make the appropriate adjustment to your submissions.
